What I did – step by step

  1. Imports. Only the libraries allowed in the brief – pandas, numpy, matplotlib, seaborn, scipy, scikit-learn – plus sqlite3, which ships with Python and is needed to actually run the SQL in Q7. I deliberately did not use statsmodels, because it is not on the list; where I needed its functionality I wrote small helpers myself (Q4).
  2. RANDOM_STATE = 42. One fixed seed, passed to every function that involves randomness: the train/test split, cross-validation folds, bootstraps, models and k-means. Re-running the notebook reproduces every number exactly, so a reviewer can verify my results.
  3. plt.rcParams.update({...}) with one fixed palette. All charts share one style, set once at the top. The colours were checked for colour-blind readability and are always used in the same order, so the same colour means the same thing everywhere.
  4. df = pd.read_csv('ifood_df.csv').

CHANNEL_COLS = ['NumWebPurchases', 'NumCatalogPurchases', 'NumStorePurchases']
PURCHASE_COLS = ['NumDealsPurchases'] + CHANNEL_COLS
CMP_COLS = ['AcceptedCmp1', 'AcceptedCmp2', 'AcceptedCmp3', 'AcceptedCmp4', 'AcceptedCmp5']
MARITAL_COLS = [c for c in df.columns if c.startswith('marital_')]

print('pandas', pd.__version__, '| scikit-learn', sklearn.__version__)

pandas 3.0.6 | scikit-learn 1.9.1

What I did – step by step

  1. Defined the column groups once, as Python lists:

    • MNT_COLS – the 6 spend columns;
    • CHANNEL_COLS – web / catalogue / store purchases;
    • PURCHASE_COLS – the channels plus deal purchases;
    • CMP_COLS – the 5 earlier campaigns;
    • MARITAL_COLS and EDU_COLS – built with [c for c in df.columns if c.startswith('marital_')], so they pick up whatever dummy columns exist.

    Why: "spend columns" then always means exactly the same 6 columns in every section – no copy-paste errors.

  2. Printed the library versions, so anyone can reproduce the environment.

Output. pandas 3.0.6, scikit-learn 1.9.1.

Q1 — Data quality & understanding¶

Task: shape, types, missing values, duplicates, the two Z_ columns, implausible values, and a summary of the issues for Marketing.

What I did – step by step

  1. df.shape → 2,205 rows, 39 columns.
  2. df.isna().sum().sum(). isna() marks every missing cell, the first sum() counts per column, the second adds the columns up – one number for the whole file.
  3. df.dtypes.value_counts() – how many columns of each data type.
  4. (df['Income'] % 1 == 0).all(). The remainder of division by 1 is 0 only for whole numbers, so this asks whether the decimal column Income actually contains only whole numbers.
  5. One overview table, one row per column, built from df.isna().sum(), df.nunique() (number of distinct values), df.min(), df.median() and df.max(). Why this layout: every column's problems are visible on one screen – n_unique = 1 exposes a constant column, and a negative minimum in a spend column is impossible.

Output and what it means.

  • 0 missing values anywhere.
  • 38 integer columns + 1 float column (Income), and every Income value is a whole number. pandas stores an integer column as float when it once had missing values, so customers without an income were most likely removed before we received the file – a silent selection step to confirm with the data owner.
  • Z_CostContact and Z_Revenue have 1 unique value each → constant columns (Q1c).
  • MntRegularProds has a minimum of −283 → impossible negative spend (checked in "pre-computed columns" below).

Q1b — Duplicates¶

In [4]:
# ═══ Q1b — Duplicates (exact, near-duplicates, conflicting labels) ═══
n_exact = int(df.duplicated().sum())
copies = df[df.duplicated(keep=False)].groupby(list(df.columns)).size().value_counts().sort_index()
print(f'Exact duplicate rows: {n_exact} ({n_exact / len(df):.1%} of the file)')
print('Records that appear more than once, by number of copies:', copies.to_dict())

FEATURES_NO_TARGET = [c for c in df.columns if c != 'Response']
n_feat_dup = int(df.duplicated(subset=FEATURES_NO_TARGET).sum())
print(f'Rows duplicated on all 38 non-target columns: {n_feat_dup} '
      f'-> {n_feat_dup - n_exact} additional rows that differ ONLY in Response')

# Near-duplicates: records identical on every column except ONE attribute (one-hot groups treated as one attribute)
distinct = df.drop_duplicates(subset=FEATURES_NO_TARGET)
attr_groups = {'marital_*': MARITAL_COLS, 'education_*': EDU_COLS,
               **{c: [c] for c in FEATURES_NO_TARGET if c not in MARITAL_COLS + EDU_COLS}}
near = {g: int(distinct.duplicated(subset=[c for c in FEATURES_NO_TARGET if c not in cols]).sum())
        for g, cols in attr_groups.items()}
print('Distinct records matching another record on everything except one attribute:', {g: n for g, n in near.items() if n})

# Could two genuinely different customers be identical on 38 columns? Even a 2-column match is rare:
pairs = distinct[distinct.duplicated(subset=['Income', 'Customer_Days'], keep=False)]
for key, g in pairs.groupby(['Income', 'Customer_Days']):
    differing = [c for c in FEATURES_NO_TARGET if g[c].nunique() > 1]
    print(f'  same (Income, Customer_Days) = {key}: the records differ in {len(differing)} columns {differing[:4]}...')

What I did – step by step

  1. df.duplicated().sum(). duplicated() marks every row that is an exact copy of an earlier row (all 39 columns equal).
  2. How many copies each record has: df[df.duplicated(keep=False)].groupby(list(df.columns)).size().value_counts(). keep=False marks all copies, including the first; grouping by every column and counting rows per group gives the number of copies.
  3. df.duplicated(subset=FEATURES_NO_TARGET).sum(). The same check on the 38 columns without Response. The difference from step 1 = rows identical on everything except the target.
  4. Near-duplicate scan: a loop that drops one attribute at a time from the subset and counts duplicates again. The one-hot groups (all marital_* columns, all education_* columns) are treated as a single attribute. Why: it reveals which attribute differs between otherwise identical records.
  5. Proof that duplicates are copies, not lookalikes: distinct.duplicated(subset=['Income', 'Customer_Days'], keep=False) – how often do genuinely different customers share even these two values (income to the unit, enrolment day)? For each such pair I list how many columns differ.

Output and what it means.

  • 184 exact duplicate rows = 8.3% of the file – 172 records appear twice and 6 appear three times.
  • 203 rows are duplicated on the 38 non-target columns → 19 extra rows that differ only in Response.
  • The near-duplicate scan finds 2 records that differ only in marital status.
  • Only one pair of genuinely different customers shares (income, enrolment day), and it differs in 18 other columns. Two different people matching on 36–38 columns is practically impossible, so all of these are copies of the same customers – most likely from a faulty join or reload upstream.

What I did – step by step

  1. dedup_exact = df.drop_duplicates() – first remove the exact copies.
  2. dedup_exact.groupby(FEATURES_NO_TARGET)['Response'].transform('nunique').gt(1):
    • groupby collects identical customer profiles (all 38 non-target columns);
    • nunique counts how many different Response values each profile has;
    • transform writes that number back onto every row (instead of one row per group), so I can filter the original rows directly;
    • .gt(1) keeps profiles with more than one value, i.e. both 0 and 1.
  3. Showed 6 example rows, sorted by income and response, so the conflict is visible.

Output and what it means. 38 rows = 19 customers, and every pair is (0, 1): the same person recorded once as "accepted the last campaign" and once as "did not". The example rows are identical in income, age, enrolment, recency and spend – only Response differs.

In [6]:
# Decision: drop exact copies; collapse each conflicting pair into ONE customer whose Response is unknown (NaN).
cleaning_log = [('Raw file', len(df))]

cust = df.drop_duplicates().copy()
cleaning_log.append(('Drop exact duplicate rows', len(cust)))

conflict = cust.groupby(FEATURES_NO_TARGET, sort=False)['Response'].transform('nunique').gt(1)
cust = cust.assign(ResponseConflict=conflict).drop_duplicates(subset=FEATURES_NO_TARGET, keep='first')
cust['Response'] = cust['Response'].astype(float).where(~cust['ResponseConflict'])   # NaN = label unknown
cleaning_log.append(('Collapse 19 conflicting pairs (label set to unknown)', len(cust)))

# 2 near-duplicates: same person on 36 columns, only the marital status differs -> keep one record
NO_MARITAL = [c for c in FEATURES_NO_TARGET if c not in MARITAL_COLS]
grp_nm = cust.groupby(NO_MARITAL, sort=False)['Response']
print('Response inside the marital near-duplicate pairs:',
      cust[cust.duplicated(subset=NO_MARITAL, keep=False)].groupby(NO_MARITAL)['Response'].agg(list).tolist())
# if the copies disagree (or one copy already had an unknown label) the label is unknown
ambiguous = (grp_nm.transform('size') > 1) & ((grp_nm.transform('nunique') > 1) | grp_nm.transform(lambda s: s.isna().any()))
cust.loc[ambiguous, ['Response', 'ResponseConflict']] = [np.nan, True]
cust = cust.drop_duplicates(subset=NO_MARITAL, keep='first')
cleaning_log.append(('Collapse 2 near-duplicates differing only in marital status', len(cust)))

print(f'Unique customers: {len(cust):,} | with a trustworthy Response label: {cust["Response"].notna().sum():,} '
      f'| response rate raw file {df["Response"].mean():.2%} vs. de-duplicated {cust["Response"].mean():.2%}')

Response inside the marital near-duplicate pairs: [[1.0, nan], [0.0, 0.0]]

Unique customers: 2,000 | with a trustworthy Response label: 1,981 | response rate raw file 15.10% vs. de-duplicated 14.69%

What I did – step by step

  1. cleaning_log = [('Raw file', 2205)]. After every step I append the step name and the row count – an audit trail of where every row went.
  2. cust = df.drop_duplicates() removes the 184 exact copies.
  3. groupby(...).transform('nunique').gt(1) flags the conflicting customers, and drop_duplicates(subset=FEATURES_NO_TARGET, keep='first') keeps one row each.
  4. cust['Response'].astype(float).where(~cust['ResponseConflict']). where keeps a value where the condition is True and puts NaN elsewhere, so the 19 conflicting customers get Response = NaN (unknown). astype(float) is needed because an integer column can't hold NaN.
  5. The 2 marital-status near-duplicates: grouped by every column except marital status, and kept one record each with drop_duplicates(subset=NO_MARITAL). If the copies disagreed on Response, or one already had an unknown label, the label becomes unknown (the printed lists show 1 such case: [1.0, nan]).

Decision on the 19 contradicting customers: one row each, label = unknown. I considered four options:

  • Drop the customer entirely – throws away valid spend and demographic data for no gain.
  • Assume they accepted – there is no evidence for it, and it would push the response rate up to ~15.5%.
  • Keep both copies – the same person with opposite labels, possibly in both train and test.
  • Label = unknown ✅ – the honest choice, because nothing in the file says which copy is true. Why NaN works technically: mean() skips NaN, and the model only uses rows where Response.notna(), so these customers drop out of everything that uses the label automatically, while their spend still counts in the EDA and the segmentation.

Why exact duplicates must go: they inflate the sample (tests become over-confident), and a copy landing in both the training and the test set lets the model "see" the answer.

Output. 2,000 unique customers, 1,981 with a trustworthy label; the response rate drops from 15.10% to 14.69%.

Q1c — Z_CostContact and Z_Revenue¶

In [7]:
# ═══ Q1c — Z_CostContact / Z_Revenue -> campaign economics ═══
print(df[['Z_CostContact', 'Z_Revenue']].agg(['nunique', 'min', 'max', 'std']))

COST_PER_CONTACT = float(df['Z_CostContact'].iloc[0])        # 3 monetary units (MU) per customer contacted
REVENUE_PER_RESPONSE = float(df['Z_Revenue'].iloc[0])        # 11 MU per customer who accepts
BREAK_EVEN_RATE = COST_PER_CONTACT / REVENUE_PER_RESPONSE     # response rate needed to cover contact costs

def campaign_pnl(n_contacted, n_responders):
    cost = n_contacted * COST_PER_CONTACT
    revenue = n_responders * REVENUE_PER_RESPONSE
    return pd.Series({'contacted': n_contacted, 'responders': n_responders,
                      'response_rate': n_responders / n_contacted, 'cost_MU': cost,
                      'revenue_MU': revenue, 'profit_MU': revenue - cost, 'ROI': (revenue - cost) / cost})

labelled = cust[cust['Response'].notna()]
pnl = pd.DataFrame({
    'Public iFood brief (2,240 customers)': pd.Series({'contacted': 2240, 'responders': 334, 'response_rate': 334 / 2240,
                                                       'cost_MU': 6720, 'revenue_MU': 3674, 'profit_MU': -3046, 'ROI': -3046 / 6720}),
    'This file, as delivered': campaign_pnl(len(df), int(df['Response'].sum())),
    'This file, de-duplicated': campaign_pnl(len(labelled), int(labelled['Response'].sum())),
}).T
print(f'Break-even response rate = {COST_PER_CONTACT:.0f} / {REVENUE_PER_RESPONSE:.0f} = {BREAK_EVEN_RATE:.1%}')
pnl.style.format({'contacted': '{:,.0f}', 'responders': '{:,.0f}', 'response_rate': '{:.1%}', 'cost_MU': '{:,.0f}',
                  'revenue_MU': '{:,.0f}', 'profit_MU': '{:,.0f}', 'ROI': '{:.0%}'})

Break-even response rate = 3 / 11 = 27.3%

  contacted responders response_rate cost_MU revenue_MU profit_MU ROI
Public iFood brief (2,240 customers) 2,240 334 14.9% 6,720 3,674 -3,046 -45%
This file, as delivered 2,205 333 15.1% 6,615 3,663 -2,952 -45%

What I did – step by step

  1. df[['Z_CostContact', 'Z_Revenue']].agg(['nunique', 'min', 'max', 'std']) – four statistics in one call. One distinct value, min = max and a standard deviation of 0 together prove a column is constant.
  2. Compared with the public iFood case brief: 2,240 customers × 3 = 6,720 campaign cost, and 334 acceptances × 11 = 3,674 revenue. Both match exactly, so these are the campaign's unit economics.
  3. Stored them as constants: COST_PER_CONTACT = 3, REVENUE_PER_RESPONSE = 11, BREAK_EVEN_RATE = 3 / 11. Why constants: they are campaign parameters, not customer attributes, and they feed every later profit calculation (Q5 thresholds, Q6 segment economics) from one place.
  4. campaign_pnl(n_contacted, n_responders) – a small function returning cost (n × 3), revenue (responders × 11), profit and ROI. I ran it for the public brief, the file as delivered and the de-duplicated file, so the three can be compared side by side.

Output and what it means.

  • Both columns are constant: 3 and 11. So it costs 3 to contact a customer, and an acceptance brings 11.
  • Break-even response rate = 3 / 11 = 27.3%. Below that, a campaign loses money.
  • All three versions of the campaign show a ~15% response rate and ROI ≈ −45% – the campaign lost almost half of what it cost (−2,952 on the delivered file).
  • Caveat: 11 is revenue, not margin, so with margin data the break-even would be even higher.
In [8]:
# Keep the economics as constants, drop the columns from the analytical table (zero variance = zero information)
cust = cust.drop(columns=['Z_CostContact', 'Z_Revenue'])

What I did. cust = cust.drop(columns=['Z_CostContact', 'Z_Revenue']) removes both columns from the analytical table.

Decision: drop them as columns, keep them as constants. A column with zero variance carries zero information for any analysis or model, but the values themselves are the most important business parameters in the case.

Q1 — Checking the pre-computed columns against the data dictionary¶

In [9]:
# ═══ Q1 (extra) — Do the pre-computed columns match the data dictionary? ═══
sum6 = df[MNT_COLS].sum(axis=1)
audit = pd.Series({
    'MntTotal = sum of all 6 categories (as documented)': (df['MntTotal'] == sum6).mean(),
    'MntTotal = sum of 5 categories, i.e. EXCLUDING gold': (df['MntTotal'] == sum6 - df['MntGoldProds']).mean(),
    'MntRegularProds = MntTotal - MntGoldProds': (df['MntRegularProds'] == df['MntTotal'] - df['MntGoldProds']).mean(),
    'MntRegularProds is negative (impossible)': (df['MntRegularProds'] < 0).mean(),
    'AcceptedCmpOverall = Cmp1..5 + Response (as documented)': (df['AcceptedCmpOverall'] == df[CMP_COLS].sum(axis=1) + df['Response']).mean(),
    'AcceptedCmpOverall = Cmp1..5 only': (df['AcceptedCmpOverall'] == df[CMP_COLS].sum(axis=1)).mean(),
    'exactly one marital_* flag = 1': (df[MARITAL_COLS].sum(axis=1) == 1).mean(),
    'exactly one education_* flag = 1': (df[EDU_COLS].sum(axis=1) == 1).mean(),
}, name='share of rows where true')
print(f'Rows with negative MntRegularProds: {(df["MntRegularProds"] < 0).sum()} (minimum = {df["MntRegularProds"].min()})')
audit.map('{:.1%}'.format).to_frame()

What I did – step by step

  1. sum6 = df[MNT_COLS].sum(axis=1). axis=1 sums across the 6 category columns, giving each customer's total.
  2. Each documented definition tested as a share of rows: e.g. (df['MntTotal'] == sum6).mean(). The comparison gives True/False per row, and the mean of True/False is the share that is True. Why this form: one number per hypothesis – 100% proves a rule, anything less shows how often it breaks.
  3. I also tested the obvious alternatives: total without gold; MntRegularProds = MntTotal − gold; AcceptedCmpOverall with and without Response; exactly one marital / education flag per row (df[MARITAL_COLS].sum(axis=1) == 1).

Output and what it means – the data dictionary is wrong in three places:

  • MntTotal = all 6 categories (as documented): only 2.8% of rows. Total without gold: 100%. So MntTotal excludes gold.
  • MntRegularProds = MntTotal − gold: 100%. Gold is therefore subtracted twice, which produces 3 negative values (minimum −283).
  • AcceptedCmpOverall including Response (as documented): 84.9%; the 5 earlier campaigns only: 100%. It does not contain the latest campaign.
  • One-hot flags: exactly one per customer in 100% of rows ✓.
In [10]:
# Fix: recompute the derived columns from their components so they match the documented definitions
cust['MntTotal'] = cust[MNT_COLS].sum(axis=1)                          # now really all 6 categories
cust['MntRegularProds'] = cust['MntTotal'] - cust['MntGoldProds']       # = the old (mislabelled) MntTotal
cust['AcceptedCmpOverall'] = cust[CMP_COLS].sum(axis=1)                 # PREVIOUS 5 campaigns only (no target inside)
assert (cust['MntRegularProds'] == df.loc[cust.index, 'MntTotal']).all()
assert (cust['MntRegularProds'] >= 0).all()
print(f'Average spend per customer: {df.loc[cust.index, "MntTotal"].mean():,.0f} MU as delivered '
      f'-> {cust["MntTotal"].mean():,.0f} MU corrected (+{cust["MntGoldProds"].mean() / df.loc[cust.index, "MntTotal"].mean():.1%})')

Average spend per customer: 564 MU as delivered -> 607 MU corrected (+7.8%)

What I did – step by step

  1. Recomputed all three columns from their components: cust[MNT_COLS].sum(axis=1), MntTotal − MntGoldProds, cust[CMP_COLS].sum(axis=1).
  2. assert checks: the new MntRegularProds must equal the old (mislabelled) MntTotal, and it must never be negative. If the fix were ever wrong, the notebook would stop instead of silently continuing.

Decision. Never trust pre-computed totals – always rebuild them from their components.

Output and what it means.

  • Average spend is 564 as delivered → 607 corrected (+7.8%): every revenue figure built on the delivered column was understated.
  • AcceptedCmpOverall doesn't leak the target as delivered. But "fixing" it to match the documentation would create a leak, which is why I rebuild it explicitly from the 5 earlier campaigns.

Q1d — Sanity checks on Age, Income, Recency¶

In [11]:

cust[['Age', 'Income', 'Recency']].describe(percentiles=[.01, .05, .25, .5, .75, .95, .99]).T.round(1)
Out[11]:
count mean std min 1% 5% 25% 50% 75% 95% 99% max
Age 2000.0 51.1 11.7 24.0 28.0 32.0 43.0 50.0 61.0 70.0 75.0 80.0
Income 2000.0 51686.2 20733.8 1730.0 7500.0 18927.0 35409.0 51445.5 68325.0 83718.8 92859.5 113734.0
Recency 2000.0 49.0 28.9 0.0 0.0 4.0 24.0 49.0 74.0 94.0 98.0 99.0

What I did. describe(percentiles=[.01, .05, .25, .5, .75, .95, .99]). Besides min and max, it shows the 1st/5th/95th/99th percentiles. Why: it tells whether an extreme value is a single isolated point or a whole tail.

Output and what it means.

  • Age: 24–80; 1% are under 28 and 1% over 75 – a smooth, plausible range.
  • Income: the minimum is 1,730, and the 1st percentile is exactly 7,500 (a suspicious round number); median ~51k, maximum ~114k. The low end needs a closer look.
  • Recency: 0–99 days, with quartiles at 24 / 49 / 74 – suspiciously evenly spread (checked properly two cells below).

How to read the numbers – a percentile is the value below which that share of customers falls: the 1st percentile of Age = 28 means 1% of customers are younger than 28; the 50th percentile is the median. Why this is useful: if the minimum is far below the 1st percentile, a few isolated values sit far from everyone else (a data-error signal); if they are close, the tail is smooth. For a perfectly even (uniform) variable from 0 to 99, the quartiles would be ~25 / 50 / 75 – almost exactly what Recency shows.

In [12]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.4))
for ax, col, bins in zip(axes, ['Age', 'Income', 'Recency'], [range(20, 85, 2), 40, range(0, 101, 5)]):
    ax.hist(cust[col], bins=bins, color=PALETTE[0], edgecolor=SURFACE, linewidth=1)
    q1, q3 = cust[col].quantile([.25, .75])
    for fence in (q1 - 1.5 * (q3 - q1), q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)):
        if cust[col].min() <= fence <= cust[col].max():
            ax.axvline(fence, color=PALETTE[7], lw=1)
    ax.axvline(cust[col].median(), color=INK2, lw=1)
    ax.set_title(col)
    ax.set_ylabel('customers')
axes[1].xaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.FuncFormatter(lambda x, _: f'{x/1000:.0f}k'))
axes[1].annotate('12 customers at exactly 7,500', xy=(7500, 25), xytext=(15000, 120), color=INK2,
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='-', color=MUTED))
fig.suptitle('Grey line = median, red line = Tukey fence (1.5 x IQR) when inside the data range', x=0.01, ha='left', color=INK2, fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

What I did. A histogram per variable (ax.hist), with a grey line at the median and red lines at the Tukey fences (Q1 − 1.5·IQR and Q3 + 1.5·IQR, from quantile([.25, .75])), drawn only if they fall inside the data range.

Why Tukey fences – and why I could use them here. Tukey's rule needs no assumption about the shape of the distribution: it is built from quartiles, and quartiles are not pulled by the extreme values themselves. The alternative, mean ± 3 standard deviations, assumes a normal distribution, and the outliers would inflate the very standard deviation used to find them.

How to read this chart

  • One panel per variable. X axis = the value (age in years, yearly income, days since the last purchase); Y axis = number of customers in each bar's range.
  • Grey vertical line = the median: half the customers are to its left, half to its right.
  • Red vertical line = a Tukey fence – drawn only if a fence falls inside the range of the data. Anything beyond a red line would be an outlier.
  • What to look for: points far from the rest, isolated spikes (one bar much taller than its neighbours) and an unexpected overall shape.

What I read from it

  • No red line in any panel → no value lies outside the Tukey fences, i.e. no classic outliers. The fences are Age 16 / 88 (data 24–80), Income −13,965 / 117,699 (data up to ~114k) and Recency −51 / 149 (data 0–99) – all outside the observed range, so they aren't drawn.
  • Age (median 50): a smooth hill, most customers between 40 and 50, a second smaller group around 60–70 – plausible, nothing to fix.
  • Income (median ~51.5k): a broad hill from ~20k to ~85k. The annotated bar at the far left is taller than its neighbours – 12 customers at exactly 7,500, a placeholder value. The few bars beyond 100k are single customers (5 people) – rare, but inside the fence.
  • Recency (median 49): every 5-day bar holds roughly 85–120 customers – a flat "wall". Real purchase recency would show a peak of recent buyers on the left and a long, falling tail to the right. This shape is what the next cell tests formally.
In [13]:
# --- Age & tenure: what date are they measured against? -----------------------------------------

chi2, p_unif = stats.chisquare(counts)

Age range 24-80 -> birth years 1940-1996 if age is also measured in 2020

What I did – step by step

  1. Which date are Age and tenure measured against?
    • Customer_Days.max() − Customer_Days.min() gives the spread of enrolment days.
    • Compared with the enrolment window of the public source data: 30-Jul-2012 to 29-Jun-2014.
    • pd.Timestamp('2014-06-29') + pd.Timedelta(days=min) reconstructs the date the days were counted to. I did the same from the oldest customer as a cross-check.
    • Then I checked whether Age fits the same reference year.
  2. Income:
    • the Tukey fences as numbers;
    • (Income < 10_000).sum();
    • Income.value_counts().head(4) – the most repeated values;
    • spend as a share of income, MntTotal / (2 × Income). Spend covers 2 years and income is yearly, so I doubled income to put both on the same period.
  3. Recency: np.histogram(Recency, bins=10, range=(0, 100)) counts customers per 10-day bin, and stats.chisquare(counts) tests whether those counts could come from a perfectly flat distribution.

Why the chi-square goodness-of-fit test – and why I could use it here

  • The question is "could these 10 bin counts come from a flat distribution?". A goodness-of-fit test answers exactly that: it compares the observed count in each category with the expected count under a hypothesis – here 1,994 / 10 ≈ 199 customers per bin.
  • What the test needs, and how this data meets it:
    • every customer counted once and independently of the others → the duplicates were removed in Q1b ✓;
    • at least 5 expected customers per bin → 199.4 ✓ (Appendix, check 3);
    • bins fixed before looking at the result → 10 equal 10-day bins ✓.
  • Alternative I did not use: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test against a uniform distribution. It assumes a continuous variable, but Recency is whole days with many ties, which makes its p-value wrong.

Output and what it means.

  • Customer_Days spans 699 days – exactly the source enrolment window – and both calculations give the same date: 27-May-2020. Age fits the same 2020 anchor (birth years 1940–1996). So ages and tenure are about 6 years too high: comparisons between customers are fine, absolute figures are not.
  • Income:
    • Tukey fences [−13,965; 117,699] – no outliers;
    • 29 incomes under 10k;
    • 7,500 appears 12 times, while the next most common value appears 3 times → a placeholder;
    • spend / income: median 0.4%, 99th percentile 1.4%, but a maximum of 35% – one customer is wildly off.
  • Recency: 189–211 customers in every 10-day bin; χ² = 3.0, p = 0.97, i.e. indistinguishable from flat. Real recency is skewed (many recent buyers, a long tail of lapsed ones), so the extract was capped at 99 days or filtered. We also don't know whether it was measured before or after the campaign – a possible leak for Q5.

How to read the numbers

  • Tukey fences = Q1 − 1.5·IQR and Q3 + 1.5·IQR, where Q1 and Q3 are the 25th and 75th percentiles and IQR = Q3 − Q1 (the range of the middle half of customers). A value outside the fences is an "outlier" by convention. Every income lies inside [−13,965; 117,699] → 0 outliers.
  • χ² = 3.0 = the sum over the bins of (observed − expected)² / expected. 0 would be perfectly flat; the larger, the less flat. With 10 bins (9 degrees of freedom) a truly random flat variable typically gives a value around 9. 3.0 is even flatter than chance usually produces.
  • p = 0.97 = the probability of bins at least this uneven if Recency really were flat. A small p (below 0.05) would reject "flat". p = 0.97 means no evidence at all against a perfectly flat distribution – and that is the warning sign, because real purchase recency is never flat.

Decision on the suspicious incomes: keep them and document them.

  • Impute – rejected: it invents data and creates a new spike at the imputed value.
  • Remove – rejected: it would also remove genuinely low-income customers and bias the base upwards.
  • Keep ✅ – the values are possible, just suspicious. In Q3c I re-run the income analysis without them to prove the conclusions don't change.

What I did – step by step

  1. Three hard business rules as True/False columns in one DataFrame:
    • R1: (MntTotal > 0) & (channel purchases == 0) – money spent without a single purchase;
    • R2: NumDealsPurchases > channel purchases – more discounted purchases than purchases in total;
    • R3: MntTotal / (2 × Income) > 0.25 – more than a quarter of income spent on food.
  2. rules.sum() counts violations per rule; rules.any(axis=1) marks a record that breaks at least one rule.
  3. Printed the flagged records to inspect them by eye.

Why rules and not an automatic outlier detector: a rule states why a record is impossible, so every removal is explainable and was defined before looking at any outcome. An automatic detector would also remove extreme-but-real customers.

Output and what it means. R1: 4, R2: 3, R3: 1 → 6 records in total. All six have an income under 10k, and most show 14–20 web visits a month or exactly 15 deal purchases – a corrupted, bot-like pattern rather than real customers.

What I did – step by step

  1. cust = cust.loc[~bad].copy() – ~ means NOT, so this keeps every record that breaks no rule.
  2. Turned cleaning_log into a table, with rows_removed computed by .diff() – the difference in row count between consecutive steps.

Decision: remove the 6 records rather than flag or "repair" them. At least one field in each must be wrong, we can't know which, and they are 0.3% of customers, all non-responders – so the response rate moves only from 14.69% to 14.73%.

Q1e — What I would tell Marketing before they trust any dashboard¶

Written for a marketing audience – no statistics needed.

What we found What it means for you What we did / what you should do
About 1 in 10 customer records is a copy (205 of 2,205 rows) Customer counts, response rates and "number of buyers" on any dashboard built on the raw file are inflated. 19 customers even appear as both "accepted" and "did not accept" the last campaign. We removed the copies → 1,994 real customers. Ask IT for a unique customer ID, so copies can't come back.
"Total spend" leaves out gold products Revenue per customer is understated by about 8% (564 → 607). Any revenue KPI or "best customers" ranking built on that column is too low. We recalculated totals from the product categories. Never use a pre-calculated total without checking how it's built.
Ages and customer tenure are counted to 2020, not to when the data was collected (2014) Everyone looks ~6 years older and ~6 years more loyal than they really were. Targeting "customers 50+" would select the wrong people. Use age only to compare groups, never as an absolute ("our average customer is 51"). Ask for the date the data was extracted.
"Days since last purchase" stops at 99 days and is suspiciously even There are no lapsed customers in this file, so it can't be used to measure churn, and we don't know whether it was recorded before or after the campaign. Treat it with care. Request the full purchase history, including inactive customers.
Some incomes are placeholders (12 customers at exactly 7,500; 23 under 10,000) Income-based segments at the low end are unreliable. Kept and flagged; we checked that our conclusions hold without them.

The one number to put on every campaign dashboard. A contact costs 3 and an acceptance brings in 11, so a campaign must reach 27% acceptance just to break even. The last campaign's 15% sounds healthy but actually lost about 45% of its cost. Report campaign profit, not only the response rate.

What you can safely use right away: what customers buy and how much, through which channels, their campaign history, family composition and education – all clean after our fixes.

Three requests to IT / the data owner:

  1. a unique customer ID;
  2. the date the extract was taken;
  3. the margin per acceptance, not just revenue.

Conclusions – Q1

  • The file needed real cleaning before any number could be trusted: 2,205 rows → 1,994 real customers (−10%), of whom 1,975 have a reliable campaign outcome. Every step is logged and explained.
  • Three pre-computed columns were wrong and are rebuilt. The two "useless" constant columns turned out to be the campaign economics: cost 3, revenue 11, break-even 27.3% – the key number for Q5 and Q6.
  • Some fields can only be used relatively: age and tenure (counted to 2020), Recency (artificially flat, timing unknown) and low incomes (placeholders).
  • Everything that follows runs on this cleaned table.

In plain words for Marketing: about one customer record in ten was a copy. Once cleaned, the real response rate is 14.7%, while each campaign needs 27% to pay for itself.

Q2 — Feature engineering¶

Task: TotalChildren, TotalPurchases, AvgSpendPerPurchase, TenureYears; collapse the education and marital dummies.

In [16]:
# ═══ Q2 — Feature engineering ═══
# a) children
cust['TotalChildren'] = cust['Kidhome'] + cust['Teenhome']
cust['HasChildren'] = (cust['TotalChildren'] > 0).astype(int)

# b) purchases: as specified, plus a version that does not double count discounted purchases
cust['TotalPurchases'] = cust[PURCHASE_COLS].sum(axis=1)          # deals + web + catalog + store (as specified)
cust['ChannelPurchases'] = cust[CHANNEL_COLS].sum(axis=1)         # web + catalog + store (each purchase counted once)

# c) average spend per purchase; 0 purchases -> NaN ("undefined"), never 0 or inf
cust['AvgSpendPerPurchase'] = cust['MntTotal'] / cust['TotalPurchases'].replace(0, np.nan)
cust['AvgSpendPerOrder'] = cust['MntTotal'] / cust['ChannelPurchases'].replace(0, np.nan)

# d) tenure: as reported (anchored to 2020) and relative to the data snapshot (what a marketer means by tenure)
DATA_ANCHOR = pd.Timestamp('2020-05-27')                          # inferred in Q1d
cust['EnrolDate'] = DATA_ANCHOR - pd.to_timedelta(cust['Customer_Days'], unit='D')
cust['TenureYears_asReported'] = (cust['Customer_Days'] / 365.25).round(2)
cust['TenureYears'] = ((cust['Customer_Days'] - cust['Customer_Days'].min()) / 365.25).round(2)

# e) collapse one-hot dummies back to single categorical columns
EDU_ORDER = ['Basic', '2n Cycle', 'Graduation', 'Master', 'PhD']
MARITAL_ORDER = ['Single', 'Together', 'Married', 'Divorced', 'Widow']
cust['Education'] = pd.Categorical(cust[EDU_COLS].idxmax(axis=1).str.replace('education_', '', regex=False),
                                   categories=EDU_ORDER, ordered=True)
cust['Marital_Status'] = pd.Categorical(cust[MARITAL_COLS].idxmax(axis=1).str.replace('marital_', '', regex=False),
                                        categories=MARITAL_ORDER)

# extra helpers used later
cust['InCouple'] = cust['Marital_Status'].isin(['Married', 'Together']).astype(int)
cust['PrevAcceptedGroup'] = pd.cut(cust['AcceptedCmpOverall'], [-1, 0, 1, 2, 10], labels=['0', '1', '2', '3+'])
cust['AgeBand'] = pd.cut(cust['Age'], [0, 39, 49, 59, 69, 120], labels=['<40', '40-49', '50-59', '60-69', '70+'])
cust['IncomeQuartile'] = pd.qcut(cust['Income'], 4, labels=['Q1 (lowest)', 'Q2', 'Q3', 'Q4 (highest)'])
for col in ['MntWines', 'MntMeatProducts', 'MntGoldProds']:
    cust[col.replace('Mnt', '').replace('Products', '').replace('Prods', '') + 'Share'] = cust[col] / cust['MntTotal']
cust['DealShare'] = cust['NumDealsPurchases'] / cust['ChannelPurchases'].replace(0, np.nan)

What I did – step by step

  1. TotalChildren = Kidhome + Teenhome, plus HasChildren = (TotalChildren > 0).astype(int). The 0/1 flag is what the Q4 tests compare (households with vs without children).
  2. TotalPurchases = cust[PURCHASE_COLS].sum(axis=1) – deals + web + catalogue + store, exactly as the task specifies.
  3. ChannelPurchases = cust[CHANNEL_COLS].sum(axis=1) – web + catalogue + store only. Why add it: a discounted purchase is still made through one of the three channels, so NumDealsPurchases is a subset of them, and adding it again counts those purchases twice.
  4. AvgSpendPerPurchase = MntTotal / TotalPurchases.replace(0, np.nan).
    • .replace(0, np.nan) turns zero purchases into "unknown" before dividing, so the result is NaN ("undefined").
    • Without it, 0 purchases would give infinity; filling with 0 would make the customer look cheap. Both are wrong.
    • It uses the corrected MntTotal, including gold. I also built AvgSpendPerOrder on ChannelPurchases.
  5. Tenure: (Customer_Days − Customer_Days.min()) / 365.25.
    • Subtracting the minimum makes the newest customer tenure 0, which removes the 2020 anchor found in Q1d; 365.25 accounts for leap years.
    • I also kept the delivered version, Customer_Days / 365.25, and reconstructed the enrolment date with pd.Timestamp('2020-05-27') - pd.to_timedelta(Customer_Days, unit='D').
  6. Collapsing the dummies: cust[EDU_COLS].idxmax(axis=1) returns, for each row, the name of the column that holds the 1 (e.g. education_PhD).
    • .str.replace('education_', '') leaves just PhD.
    • pd.Categorical(..., categories=[...], ordered=True) fixes the order Basic → 2n Cycle → Graduation → Master → PhD, so tables and charts are sorted logically.
    • The same for marital status.
  7. Extra helper columns for later sections: InCouple, PrevAcceptedGroup (0 / 1 / 2 / 3+ earlier acceptances, via pd.cut), AgeBand, IncomeQuartile (pd.qcut – 4 equal-sized income groups), spend shares and DealShare.

Output. No printed output – the columns are created here and checked in the next cell.

In [17]:
# Validation: every engineered field is checked, not just created
assert (cust['TotalChildren'].between(0, 4)).all()
assert cust['Education'].notna().all() and cust['Marital_Status'].notna().all()
assert (pd.get_dummies(cust['Education'], prefix='education', prefix_sep='_').astype(int)[EDU_COLS].values
        == cust[EDU_COLS].values).all(), 'education round-trip failed'
assert (pd.get_dummies(cust['Marital_Status'], prefix='marital', prefix_sep='_').astype(int)[MARITAL_COLS].values
        == cust[MARITAL_COLS].values).all(), 'marital round-trip failed'
print('Zero-purchase customers (AvgSpendPerPurchase undefined):', int(cust['AvgSpendPerPurchase'].isna().sum()),

print('EnrolDate range:', cust['EnrolDate'].min().date(), '->', cust['EnrolDate'].max().date())

What I did – step by step. Every new field is validated with assert – the notebook stops if a check fails:

  1. TotalChildren is between 0 and 4.
  2. No missing education or marital categories.
  3. Round-trip test: pd.get_dummies(cust['Education']) must reproduce the original education_* columns exactly, and the same for marital status. That proves collapsing the dummies lost nothing.
  4. Counted the zero-purchase customers, and printed the reconstructed enrolment-date range.
  5. describe() of the new columns, and counts per category.

Output and what it means.

  • 0 zero-purchase customers now. The 2 in the raw file were among the impossible records removed in Q1; the NaN rule stays in place for new data.
  • Enrolment dates run from exactly 30-Jul-2012 to 29-Jun-2014 – the source window, which also confirms the 2020 anchor.
  • Median TotalPurchases is 15 vs 12 for ChannelPurchases. So the specified average basket (median 23.7) understates the real one (median 29.9) by ~20%. That matters for the $30 free-delivery design in Q4c, where the threshold sits right at the median basket.
  • Tenure is 0–1.9 years (median ~1), instead of the misleading 5.9–7.8 years as delivered.
  • Small groups: Basic education 49, Widow 69 – their numbers will have wide confidence intervals later. "2n Cycle" is the Bologna second cycle (≈ Master level), so its position in the order is ambiguous; I kept it as a separate category rather than guess.

Conclusions – Q2

  • All requested fields exist and are validated. Two definitions were improved and documented:
    • purchases counted without double-counting discounted ones;
    • tenure measured from the newest customer instead of from 2020.
  • The real average basket is ~30 per order, not ~24 – relevant for any minimum-order or free-delivery threshold.

In plain words for Marketing: a typical customer orders for about 30 per order, has been with us about 1 year, and 72% of customers have children at home.

Q3 — Exploratory analysis & storytelling¶

Task: distributions; which segments spend most and how the mix differs; income vs spend; three slides for the Head of Marketing.

Q3a — Distributions¶

What I did – step by step

  1. One table of shape statistics for Income, Age, total spend and log10(spend):

    • mean() and median();
    • skew() – asymmetry;
    • kurt() – heaviness of the tails (excess kurtosis);
    • the share of customers below the mean, (dist < dist.mean()).mean().

    Why the last one: if far more than 50% of customers are below the mean, the mean is pulled up by a minority.

  2. Four histograms with a mean line (orange) and a median line (grey), including spend on a log scale. Why log: spend is money – multiplicative – and a log scale shows its real shape.

  3. Bimodality test: GaussianMixture(k).fit(log-spend) for k = 1 and k = 2, compared with .bic(). n_init=5 restarts the fit 5 times to avoid a poor solution.

Why a Gaussian mixture with BIC – and why I could use it here

  • The question: is log-spend one group or two? A Gaussian mixture describes the data as a blend of normal "bumps"; comparing 1 bump with 2 bumps answers the question directly.
  • BIC (Bayesian information criterion) rewards a better fit but penalises every extra parameter, so a second bump wins only if it describes the data much better. It is valid for comparing models fitted by maximum likelihood on the same data ✓.
  • Assumption: each bump is roughly normal on the log scale – the log-spend histogram shows two clear hills, each roughly bell-shaped ✓. On the raw scale this would fail (the raw histogram is a spike plus a long tail).

How to read this chart

  • Four histograms. X axis = the value; Y axis = number of customers in each bar.
  • Orange line = mean, grey line = median. If they coincide, the distribution is symmetric. If the mean sits to the right of the median, a minority of large values pulls the average up.
  • The fourth panel shows spend on a log scale (10 → 100 → 1,000 equally spaced), which spreads out the crowded low values.

What I read from it

  • Income and Age: mean and median almost on top of each other (51.8k vs 51.5k; 51 vs 50) → symmetric; the average describes the typical customer well.
  • Total spend (raw): a tall spike at the left – 31% of customers spent less than 100 in two years – and a long tail to ~2,500. The mean (608) sits far to the right of the median (398): the average is pulled up by heavy buyers.
  • Log spend: two hills – one around ~60 and one around ~850, with a dip in between. That is two kinds of customers, not one.

Output and what it means.

  • Income (skew 0.02) and age (0.09) are symmetric: mean ≈ median.
  • Spend: mean 608 vs median 398, skew 0.86, and 59% of customers are below the mean.
  • On the log scale: BIC 3,213 with two components vs 3,896 with one, with centres at ~61 (42% of customers) and ~845 (58%). These are two populations: light and heavy buyers.
  • "The average customer" does not exist. I therefore report medians and segments, and use log-spend in the models.

How to read the numbers

  • Skewness: 0 = symmetric; positive = long right tail. Roughly: below 0.5 fairly symmetric, 0.5–1 moderately skewed, above 1 strongly skewed. Spend 0.86 → moderately-to-strongly skewed.
  • Excess kurtosis: 0 = tails like a normal distribution; negative = flatter, with lighter tails (Income −0.85 and Age −0.81 are flat-topped, with no extreme values).
  • share_below_mean: 0.50 for a symmetric variable. 0.59 for spend → the mean is above the typical customer.
  • BIC: lower = better. A difference above 10 is considered very strong evidence; here the difference is 683 → overwhelming evidence for two groups.

Q3b — Which segments spend the most, and does the mix differ?¶

# ═══ Q3b — Segments: who spends most, and the spend mix ═══
def segment_table(col):
    g = cust.groupby(col, observed=True)
    t = pd.DataFrame({
        'customers': g.size(),
        'mean_spend': g['MntTotal'].mean(),
        'median_spend': g['MntTotal'].median(),
        'mean_income': g['Income'].mean(),
        'share_of_customers': g.size() / len(cust),
        'share_of_revenue': g['MntTotal'].sum() / cust['MntTotal'].sum(),
    })
    t['revenue_index'] = 100 * t['share_of_revenue'] / t['share_of_customers']   # >100 = over-indexes on revenue
    return t

  • number of customers;

# Which dimension separates spenders the most? Kruskal-Wallis (rank-based: spend is very skewed) + effect size
rows = []
for col in ['Education', 'Marital_Status', 'InCouple', 'TotalChildren', 'HasChildren']:
    groups = [g['MntTotal'].to_numpy() for _, g in cust.groupby(col, observed=True)]
    H, p = stats.kruskal(*groups)
    k, n = len(groups), len(cust)
    rows.append({'segmentation': col, 'groups': k, 'H': H, 'p_value': p, 'eta2_H': (H - k + 1) / (n - k)})
kw = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('segmentation').sort_values('eta2_H', ascending=False)
kw.style.format({'H': '{:.1f}', 'p_value': '{:.1e}', 'eta2_H': '{:.3f}'})

  groups H p_value eta2_H
segmentation        
TotalChildren 4 513.0 7.3e-111 0.256
HasChildren 2 456.6 2.7e-101 0.229
Education 5 65.4 2.1e-13 0.031
Marital_Status 5 5.7 2.2e-01 0.001
InCouple 2 0.9 3.3e-01 -0.000

What I did. stats.kruskal(*groups) for five ways of splitting customers (number of children, has children yes/no, education, marital status, in a couple yes/no), with the effect size η² = (H − k + 1) / (n − k) (H = test statistic, k = number of groups, n = customers), sorted from the strongest to the weakest.

Why Kruskal-Wallis – and why I could use it here

  • The question: do several groups (e.g. 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 children) differ in spend? The textbook test is one-way ANOVA, but ANOVA assumes that spend is normally distributed with the same variance in every group. Neither holds: spend is right-skewed with two humps (Q3a), and childless customers vary far more than families. ANOVA's p-values would be unreliable.
  • Kruskal-Wallis replaces every spend value by its rank (1 = lowest spender … 1,994 = highest) and tests whether the average rank differs between groups. What it needs, and how this data meets it:
    • independent observations – one row per customer ✓ (Q1b);
    • an outcome that can be put in order – spend ✓;
    • enough customers per group for the χ² approximation of H (≥ 5) – the smallest group has 45 (3 children) ✓;
    • ties are allowed – scipy applies the tie correction automatically ✓.
  • What it does not need: normality or equal variances – exactly the assumptions that fail here.
  • How I interpret it: because the groups have different shapes, I read a significant result as "customers in some groups tend to spend more" (stochastic dominance), not strictly "the medians differ".

Output and what it means.

  • Number of children η² = 0.26 – by far the strongest separator (H = 513, p = 7·10⁻¹¹¹).
  • Education 0.03 – real (p = 2·10⁻¹³), but small.
  • Marital status 0.00 (p = 0.22) – not even significant; "in a couple" the same (p = 0.33).

Household composition explains spending; marital status does not.

How to read the numbers

  • H – how far apart the groups' average ranks are. 0 = identical; the bigger, the more different. If the groups really spent the same, H would behave like a χ² variable with k − 1 degrees of freedom – for 4 groups a value around 3 is normal. 513 is enormous.
  • p-value – the probability of differences at least this large if all groups really spent the same. Below 0.05 = "statistically significant", i.e. unlikely to be chance. Children 7·10⁻¹¹¹ and education 2·10⁻¹³ → real. Marital status 0.22 → a difference of that size appears by chance 22% of the time → not significant.
  • η² (eta squared) – the share of the differences between customers' spend ranks that the grouping explains, from 0 (knowing the group tells you nothing) to 1 (the group explains everything). Rule of thumb: 0.01 = small, 0.06 = medium, 0.14 = large.
    • number of children 0.256 → large: about a quarter of the rank differences between customers is explained just by how many children they have;
    • has children yes/no 0.229 → large – nearly all of it is the yes/no split;
    • education 0.031 → small;
    • marital status 0.001 and "in a couple" −0.000 → none. A slightly negative value is just the formula's small-sample correction around zero; read it as 0.
  • Why I rank by η² and not by p: with ~2,000 customers even tiny differences get small p-values. p answers "is it real?", η² answers "is it big?" – and Marketing needs the second.
In [21]:
def boot_mean_ci(x, n_boot=4000, seed=RANDOM_STATE):
    x = np.asarray(x, float)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    means = x[rng.integers(0, len(x), size=(n_boot, len(x)))].mean(axis=1)
    return np.percentile(means, [2.5, 97.5])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.2), sharex=True)
for ax, col in zip(axes, ['Education', 'Marital_Status', 'TotalChildren']):
    levels = [lvl for lvl in (cust[col].cat.categories if hasattr(cust[col], 'cat') else sorted(cust[col].unique()))]
    for i, lvl in enumerate(levels):
        x = cust.loc[cust[col] == lvl, 'MntTotal']
        lo, hi = boot_mean_ci(x)
        ax.plot([lo, hi], [i, i], color=PALETTE[0], lw=2, solid_capstyle='round')
        ax.plot(x.mean(), i, 'o', color=PALETTE[0], ms=7, mec=SURFACE, mew=1.5)
        ax.text(hi + 25, i, f'{x.mean():,.0f}  (n={len(x)})', va='center', color=INK2, fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(levels)))
    ax.set_yticklabels([str(l) for l in levels])
    ax.invert_yaxis()
    ax.set_title(f'Mean 2-year spend by {col}')
    ax.axvline(cust['MntTotal'].mean(), color=MUTED, lw=1)
axes[0].set_xlabel('MU (dot = mean, line = 95% bootstrap CI, grey = overall mean)')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

What I did. boot_mean_ci() – a bootstrap confidence interval for each group's mean:

  • draw 4,000 resamples of the group with replacement (rng.integers row indices, vectorised for speed);
  • compute the mean of each resample;
  • take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.

Plotted as a dot (mean) with a line (95% CI) per group, and a grey vertical line for the overall mean.

Why a bootstrap confidence interval – and why I could use it here

  • The usual formula (mean ± 1.96 × standard error) assumes the mean is normally distributed; for skewed spend in small groups (45–69 customers) that is shaky. The bootstrap uses the data's own variability instead – no formula and no normality assumption.
  • What it needs: independent customers ✓ (one row each) and a group large enough to represent its population. That holds for the large groups; for the smallest ones (3 children: 45, Basic: 49, Widow: 69) the interval is a little too narrow, so I treat them with caution.

How to read this chart

  • One row per group. The dot is the group's mean 2-year spend; the number next to it repeats the mean and the group size n.

  • The horizontal line through the dot is the 95% confidence interval – the range in which the group's true mean plausibly lies. A short line = a precise estimate (a large group); a long line = an uncertain one (a small group).

  • The grey vertical line is the overall mean (608) of all customers.

  • Rules for reading it:

    • two lines that don't overlap → the two groups clearly differ;
    • lines that overlap a lot → the data can't tell the groups apart;
    • a line entirely on one side of the grey line → that group differs from the average customer;
    • a line that crosses the grey line → the group may well be average.

    (Non-overlap is a strict rule: slightly overlapping intervals can still be significantly different – the formal tests are in the previous cell.)

What I read from it – panel by panel

  • Education: Basic (84, CI 55–125) sits alone far to the left – clearly below everyone. 2n Cycle (493, CI 415–571) lies entirely left of the grey line → below average. Graduation (627, 591–664), Master (611, 544–681) and PhD (671, 615–731) overlap each other → no clear difference between the three higher degrees; PhD is just above average.
  • Marital status: all five lines overlap each other and cross (or touch) the grey line → no group differs. Widow has the highest dot (744) but also the longest line (608–881) because there are only 69 widows – its lower end touches the overall mean, so even that isn't a clear difference.
  • Number of children: 0 children: 1,123 (CI 1,070–1,175) – far right of everything; 1 child: 471 (443–499); 2 children: 250 (218–283); 3 children: 259 (144–391). The lines for 0, 1 and 2 don't overlap → each step from 0 to 1 to 2 children is a clear drop. The lines for 2 and 3 overlap → no difference between 2 and 3 children (and only 45 customers have 3).

Output and what it means. Children separate spend clearly, education only at the low end (Basic, 2n Cycle), marital status not at all – the same ranking as the η² in the previous cell, now visible with its uncertainty.

# Spend MIX: share of wallet = category spend / total spend of the segment (revenue-weighted)
CAT_LABELS = {'MntWines': 'Wine', 'MntFruits': 'Fruit', 'MntMeatProducts': 'Meat', 'MntFishProducts': 'Fish',
              'MntSweetProducts': 'Sweets', 'MntGoldProds': 'Gold'}

def wallet_share(col):
    s = cust.groupby(col, observed=True)[MNT_COLS].sum()
    return s.div(s.sum(axis=1), axis=0).rename(columns=CAT_LABELS)

overall_share = (cust[MNT_COLS].sum() / cust[MNT_COLS].sum().sum()).rename(CAT_LABELS)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 3.4), sharex=True)
for ax, col in zip(axes, ['Education', 'Marital_Status', 'TotalChildren']):
    ws = wallet_share(col)
    left = np.zeros(len(ws))
    for j, cat in enumerate(ws.columns):
        ax.barh(range(len(ws)), ws[cat], left=left, color=PALETTE[j], edgecolor=SURFACE, linewidth=2, height=0.7,
                label=cat)
        for i, (l, w) in enumerate(zip(left, ws[cat])):
            if w >= 0.09:
                ax.text(l + w / 2, i, f'{w:.0%}', ha='center', va='center', color='white', fontsize=8)
        left += ws[cat].to_numpy()
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(ws)))
    ax.set_yticklabels([str(i) for i in ws.index])
    ax.invert_yaxis()
    ax.grid(False)
    ax.set_title(f'Share of wallet by {col}')

What I did – step by step

  1. Share of wallet: groupby(col)[MNT_COLS].sum() divided by each group's row total (div(s.sum(axis=1), axis=0)). That is a revenue-weighted mix – where the group's money actually goes, rather than an average of individual percentages, which small spenders would distort.
  2. Stacked 100% bars per group, with labels only on segments ≥ 9%, so the chart stays readable.
  3. Index vs the average customer: each share divided by the overall share × 100, shown as a coloured table – blue below average, red above.

(Descriptive shares and indices – no test, so nothing to assume. Small groups – Basic 49, Widow 69, 3 children 45 – have noisier mixes.)

How to read this chart

  • One bar per group, always 100% long. Each coloured piece is the share of that group's total spend going to one category (colours in the legend: wine, fruit, meat, fish, sweets, gold).
  • Compare the length of the same colour across bars: a longer blue piece = that group spends a larger share on wine – not necessarily more money (a small wallet can have a large wine share).
  • The labelled percentages are the biggest pieces; small pieces are unlabelled to keep it readable – their exact values are in the index table.

How to read the index table – 100 = the same share as the average customer; 120 = a 20% larger share than average; 50 = half the average share.

What I read from it

  • Overall: wine is 50.5% of revenue, meat 27.2%; fish, gold, sweets and fruit are 4–7% each.
  • Education: the blue (wine) piece grows steadily from Basic 9% → 2n Cycle 41% → Graduation 46% → Master 55% → PhD 61%. Basic is a different basket altogether: wine 9% (index 18), but gold 27%, fish 21% and sweets 15% (indices 333–376).
  • Marital status: the five bars look almost identical (wine 48–53%, meat 25–30%) → marital status doesn't change the mix (indices within ±10%).
  • Children: with more children the wine share rises (45% → 57% → 57% → 62%) and the meat share falls (33% → 21% → 21% → 24%). Childless households over-index on meat (122) and fish (111); families on wine (112–123) and gold (119–144).

Output and what it means. Families put a bigger share of a smaller wallet into wine and gold; childless households buy a richer food basket (meat, fish). Education changes the mix strongly only at the Basic level; marital status not at all.

Q3c — Income vs total spend¶

What I did – step by step

  1. stats.spearmanr(Income, MntTotal) and stats.pearsonr(...) side by side.
  2. stats.linregress(np.log(Income), np.log(MntTotal)). In a log-log regression the slope is the elasticity: the % change in spend for a 1% change in income. 1.1 ** slope − 1 converts it into "+10% income → +x% spend".
  3. The same Spearman correlation within each children group (groupby('KidsGroup')).
  4. Holding income constant without a model: pd.qcut(Income, 10) creates 10 equal-sized income bands (deciles), then groupby([IncomeDecile, HasChildren])['MntTotal'].median().unstack(). Comparing families and non-families within the same decile removes most of the income difference between them. I used the median because spend is skewed.
  5. Spend as a share of income per income quartile: (MntTotal / 2) / Income, median per quartile.

Why these methods – and why I could use them here

  • Spearman's ρ (main measure) – does spend tend to rise when income rises? It works on ranks, so it captures any monotonic relationship (straight or curved) and isn't pulled by the long tail of big spenders. Needs: pairs measured on the same customer ✓, independent customers ✓, values that can be ordered ✓. No normality needed.
  • Pearson's r (for comparison only) – measures a straight-line relationship and is sensitive to extreme values. Its p-value formally assumes bivariate normality, but with 1,994 customers the central limit theorem makes it reliable. I report it next to Spearman because r below ρ signals a curved relationship.
  • Log-log regression – needs positive values (every customer here has income > 0 and spend > 0 ✓, so the logs exist) and a roughly straight relationship on the log scale (R² 0.61 below). I use only the slope, not its p-value, so the assumptions about the residuals (normal, equal spread) don't affect the conclusion; the next cell re-checks the slope without the suspicious incomes.
  • Medians within income deciles – no model at all, so there is nothing to assume. Comparing inside the same decile controls for income by design.

Output and what it means.

  • Spearman 0.86, Pearson 0.82 – strong, but not purely linear.
  • Elasticity 2.37 (R² 0.61): +10% income → about +25% spend.
  • Spend as a share of income rises from 0.11% in the lowest quartile to 0.86% in the highest – these products behave like "luxury" goods.
  • Decile table: at the same income, families spend far less – decile 3: 66 vs 290; decile 6: 482 vs 939. The gap is largest in the middle and smaller at the extremes.

How to read the numbers

  • ρ and r run from −1 to +1: 0 = no relationship, +1 = perfectly rising together, −1 = one rises as the other falls. Rule of thumb: about 0.1 weak, 0.3 moderate, 0.5 and above strong. 0.86 = very strong. ρ (0.86) > r (0.82) → strongly rising, but along a curve rather than a straight line.
  • Elasticity 2.37 – +1% income goes with +2.37% spend. Above 1 means spend grows faster than income (economists call that a luxury good); below 1 would be a necessity. +10% income → 1.1^2.37 − 1 ≈ +25% spend.
  • R² = 0.61 – income explains 61% of the variation in (log) spend; 0 = nothing, 1 = everything. The remaining 39% is family, habits and everything else.
  • ratio_with_vs_without in the table – the median spend of families ÷ that of non-families in the same decile. 1.00 = the same; 0.50 = families spend half.

How to read this chart

What I read from it

  • Scatter: below ~40k income almost everyone spends little (median 56); spend takes off between 40k and 60k (median 316) and is high above 60k (median 1,179) – a curve bending upwards, not a straight line.
  • The top of the cloud is mostly blue: of the 217 customers who spent 1,500 or more, 79% have no children, although only 28% of all customers are childless. Orange and green dots stay low even at 60–80k income.
  • Lines: the orange line is below the blue one at every income level. The gap is small in the lowest decile (50 vs 55) and in the top decile (1,395 vs 1,566), and widest in the middle – e.g. at ~36k: 66 vs 291, at ~55k: 482 vs 939. Both lines climb steeply from ~45k, the blue one earlier.

Output and what it means. Spend rises steeply with income, but income alone overestimates what families spend – at the same income they spend less in every decile – up to 77% less (decile 3).

# Robustness for the Q1d decision to KEEP suspicious incomes: do the income conclusions change without them?

    rows.append({'sample': label, 'customers': len(d),

                 'income elasticity (log-log)': stats.linregress(np.log(d['Income']), np.log(d['MntTotal'])).slope,
                 'spend ratio with/without children (mean over deciles)': ratio.mean()})
print(f'Suspicious incomes in the cleaned table: {suspicious_income.sum()} below 10k '

What I did. A robustness check for the Q1d decision to keep the suspicious incomes. The same three numbers – Spearman, elasticity, and the children spend ratio averaged over deciles – computed once on all customers and once on cust[~(Income < 10_000)].

Why this check – and why it is enough. A decision about questionable data is only safe if the conclusions don't depend on it. Re-running the key numbers with and without the 23 doubtful customers (a sensitivity analysis) tests exactly that, with no extra assumptions: the methods are the same as in the previous cell.

Output and what it means.

  • Without the 23 low incomes, Spearman stays 0.86 and the children ratio stays ~0.63 – the conclusions don't depend on those customers, which justifies keeping them.
  • Only the elasticity moves (2.37 → 2.71), so I quote it as "about 2.4–2.7", not as one exact number.

How to read the table – compare the two rows column by column. A number that barely changes is robust; a number that moves (the elasticity) is sensitive to a few customers, so I report it as a range. The children ratio 0.63 means families spend on average 63% of what non-families in the same income decile spend.

Q3d — Three slides for the Head of Marketing¶

# Slide 1 — revenue concentration (Pareto)
s = cust['MntTotal'].sort_values(ascending=False).to_numpy()
cum_rev = s.cumsum() / s.sum()
cum_cust = np.arange(1, len(s) + 1) / len(s)
top = {q: cum_rev[int(np.ceil(q * len(s))) - 1] for q in (0.1, 0.2, 0.5)}
bottom50 = 1 - top[0.5]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
ax.plot(cum_cust, cum_rev, color=PALETTE[0])
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color=AXIS, lw=1)
for q, txt_off in [(0.1, (0.06, -0.10)), (0.2, (0.08, -0.08)), (0.5, (0.07, -0.12))]:
    ax.plot(q, top[q], 'o', color=PALETTE[0], ms=7, mec=SURFACE, mew=1.5)
    ax.annotate(f'Top {q:.0%} of customers\n= {top[q]:.0%} of revenue', xy=(q, top[q]),
                xytext=(q + txt_off[0], top[q] + txt_off[1]), color=INK, fontsize=9)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(1))
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(1))
ax.set_xlabel('Customers, ranked from highest to lowest 2-year spend')
ax.set_ylabel('Cumulative share of revenue')
ax.set_title(f'The top 20% of customers bring in {top[0.2]:.0%} of revenue; the bottom half only {bottom50:.0%}')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

How. MntTotal.sort_values(ascending=False), then cumsum() / sum() gives the cumulative share of revenue as we go down the customer list; I read it off at 10%, 20% and 50% of customers. The grey diagonal shows what perfect equality would look like. (A cumulative-revenue curve, also called a Pareto or Lorenz-type curve – no test involved, so there are no assumptions to check.)

How to read this chart

  • X axis: customers sorted from the biggest spender (left) to the smallest (right), as a share of all customers.
  • Y axis: the share of total revenue those customers bring in, adding up as you move right.
  • Blue curve = the real data. Grey diagonal = perfect equality: if everyone spent the same, 20% of customers would bring 20% of revenue.
  • How to use it: pick a point on the X axis, go up to the blue curve, read the value on the Y axis. The further the curve bows above the diagonal, the more concentrated revenue is.

What I read from it

  • At 10% on the X axis the curve is at 30% → the top 10% of customers bring 30% of revenue – three times their share.
  • At 20% → 52%: one customer in five brings more than half of revenue (close to the classic 80/20 pattern, here "20/52").
  • At 50% → 91%: so the other half of customers brings only 9%.
  • After about 60% the curve is almost flat (95% at 60%, 98% at 70%, 99% at 80%): the last 40% of customers add only ~5% of revenue.

So what: protecting the top fifth is worth more than another mass discount.

Within each band I compare the median spend of households with and without children, with bar labels showing the values. (Medians within bands – a descriptive comparison with nothing to assume; the formal tests are in Q4.)

How to read this chart

  • X axis: five income bands from the lowest 20% to the top 20% of household income.
  • Bars: the median 2-year spend of customers without children (blue) and with children (orange) in the same income band – the typical customer, not pulled by a few big spenders.
  • How to use it: compare the two bars within one band. Because both groups have similar incomes there, the gap can't be explained by income.

What I read from it

  • Every orange bar is lower than the blue bar next to it – in all five bands.
  • 60–80% band: 825 vs 1,197 → families spend 31% less (ratio 0.69) – the example in the title.
  • The biggest relative gap is in the 20–40% band: 81 vs 290 (ratio 0.28, −72%).
  • The smallest gaps are at the extremes: lowest 20% (48 vs 66, ratio 0.72) and top 20% (1,179 vs 1,478, ratio 0.80).

So what: at the same income, families spend 20–72% less (ratios 0.72 / 0.28 / 0.54 / 0.69 / 0.80 from the lowest band to the top). Income-based targeting overestimates them: offers to families should build the basket, not push premium wine.

How. groupby('PrevAcceptedGroup')['Response'].agg(['mean', 'size']) – the response rate to the latest campaign by how many of the 5 earlier campaigns the customer accepted, with the red break-even line at 27.3% and the group sizes under the bars. (Observed rates – no model. For the reading below I also computed a Wilson 95% interval for each bar, the interval method explained in Q4.)

How to read this chart

  • X axis: how many of the 5 earlier campaigns the customer accepted (0, 1, 2, 3 or more).
  • Bar height and bold label: the share of those customers who accepted the latest campaign.
  • Under each bar: how many customers are in the group and their share of the base – a high bar over a tiny group matters less for the business than a low bar over a big one.
  • Red horizontal line = break-even 27.3%. A bar above it means contacting that whole group makes money; below it, every contact loses money on average.

What I read from it

  • 0 earlier acceptances: 8% (95% CI 6.7–9.4%) – far below the red line, and this is 79% of the base (1,564 customers). Mass mailing pays for these contacts and gets little back.
  • 1 earlier acceptance: 30% (CI 25–36%) – just above the line on average, but the interval reaches below 27.3%, so this group is roughly break-even, not a sure win.
  • 2: 52% (CI 41–63%) and 3+: 82% (CI 69–90%) – clearly above break-even, but only 4% + 3% of customers.
  • The rate climbs at every step – a strong, monotonic signal, which is why campaign history becomes the top driver in the Q5 model.

So what: stop mass mailing and concentrate on customers with a track record – and use the model (Q5) to find the profitable ones among the 79% with no history.

Conclusions – Q3

  • Spending is very unequal: two populations (light buyers ~60, heavy buyers ~850), and the top 20% of customers bring in 52% of revenue.
  • Family composition is the strongest spend driver – much stronger than education, while marital status plays no role. Childless households (28% of customers) bring in 52% of revenue.
  • Spend rises steeply with income (+10% income ≈ +25% spend), but at the same income families spend 20–72% less.
  • Wine (50%) and meat (27%) are the core categories. Families shift spend towards wine and gold; childless households towards meat and fish.
  • Past acceptance is a powerful signal: 8% response with no history vs 30–82% with it.

In plain words for Marketing:

  • Focus effort on a small group of high-value, mostly childless customers.
  • Build value offers (bundles, family meals) for families.
  • Plan product messages by family stage, not by marital status.
  • Target people who said "yes" before.

Q4 — Statistical testing & experimentation¶

Task: test Marketing's claims about families (wine spend, responsiveness) and about complainers; design an A/B test.

In [29]:
# ═══ Q4 — Statistical helper functions ═══
# ---------- Statistical helpers (all built on scipy/numpy; each one is verified against textbook formulas) ----------
Z975 = stats.norm.ppf(0.975)

def wilson_ci(k, n, alpha=0.05):
    z = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2)
    p = k / n
    centre = (p + z**2 / (2 * n)) / (1 + z**2 / n)
    half = z * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z**2 / (4 * n**2)) / (1 + z**2 / n)
    return centre - half, centre + half

def newcombe_diff_ci(k1, n1, k2, n2):
    """95% CI for p1 - p2 (Newcombe hybrid score method; reliable even for small groups)."""
    p1, p2 = k1 / n1, k2 / n2
    l1, u1 = wilson_ci(k1, n1)
    l2, u2 = wilson_ci(k2, n2)
    d = p1 - p2
    return d - np.sqrt((p1 - l1) ** 2 + (u2 - p2) ** 2), d + np.sqrt((u1 - p1) ** 2 + (p2 - l2) ** 2)

def compare_proportions(k1, n1, k2, n2):
    """Group 1 vs group 2 on a binary outcome: tests + every effect size a stakeholder might ask for."""
    table = np.array([[k1, n1 - k1], [k2, n2 - k2]])
    chi2, p_chi2, _, expected = stats.chi2_contingency(table, correction=False)   # == two-proportion z-test
    _, p_fisher = stats.fisher_exact(table)
    rr = stats.contingency.relative_risk(k1, n1, k2, n2)
    orr = stats.contingency.odds_ratio(table, kind='sample')
    p1, p2 = k1 / n1, k2 / n2
    return pd.Series({
        'n_group1': n1, 'rate_group1': p1, 'n_group2': n2, 'rate_group2': p2,
        'diff_pp': 100 * (p1 - p2), 'diff_CI95_pp': tuple(np.round(100 * np.array(newcombe_diff_ci(k1, n1, k2, n2)), 1)),
        'relative_risk': rr.relative_risk, 'RR_CI95': tuple(np.round(rr.confidence_interval(), 2)),
        'odds_ratio': orr.statistic, 'OR_CI95': tuple(np.round(orr.confidence_interval(), 2)),
        'cohens_h': 2 * np.arcsin(np.sqrt(p1)) - 2 * np.arcsin(np.sqrt(p2)),
        'p_chi2': p_chi2, 'p_fisher': p_fisher, 'min_expected_count': expected.min(),
    })

def logit_inference(X, y):
    """Unpenalised logistic regression via Newton-Raphson, with Wald SEs, p-values and odds ratios."""
    Xc = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), np.asarray(X, float)])
    y = np.asarray(y, float)
    beta = np.zeros(Xc.shape[1])
    for _ in range(100):
        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-Xc @ beta))
        H = Xc.T @ (Xc * (p * (1 - p))[:, None])
        step = np.linalg.solve(H, Xc.T @ (y - p))
        beta += step
        if np.abs(step).max() < 1e-10:
            break
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-Xc @ beta))
    se = np.sqrt(np.diag(np.linalg.inv(Xc.T @ (Xc * (p * (1 - p))[:, None]))))
    out = pd.DataFrame({'coef': beta, 'se': se}, index=['const'] + list(X.columns))
    out['p_value'] = 2 * stats.norm.sf(np.abs(out['coef'] / out['se']))
    out['odds_ratio'] = np.exp(out['coef'])
    out['OR_low'], out['OR_high'] = np.exp(out['coef'] - Z975 * out['se']), np.exp(out['coef'] + Z975 * out['se'])
    return out

def ols_robust(X, y):
    """OLS with heteroscedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors."""
    Xc = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), np.asarray(X, float)])
    y = np.asarray(y, float)
    XtX_inv = np.linalg.inv(Xc.T @ Xc)
    beta = XtX_inv @ Xc.T @ y
    e = y - Xc @ beta
    n, k = Xc.shape
    cov = XtX_inv @ (Xc.T @ (Xc * (e ** 2)[:, None])) @ XtX_inv * n / (n - k)
    out = pd.DataFrame({'coef': beta, 'se': np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))}, index=['const'] + list(X.columns))
    out['p_value'] = 2 * stats.t.sf(np.abs(out['coef'] / out['se']), df=n - k)
    return out

def holm(pvals):
    """Holm-Bonferroni adjusted p-values (controls the family-wise error rate)."""
    p = np.asarray(pvals, float)
    order = np.argsort(p)
    adj = np.empty_like(p)
    running = 0.0
    for rank, i in enumerate(order):
        running = max(running, min(1.0, (len(p) - rank) * p[i]))
        adj[i] = running
    return adj

What I did – the helper functions, and why each exists. statsmodels is not on the allowed list, so I built the pieces I needed from numpy and scipy:

  1. wilson_ci(k, n) – a confidence interval for a proportion (Wilson score formula). Why: the textbook interval (p ± 1.96·SE) is wrong for small groups or rates near 0, and I need it for 19 complainers.
  2. newcombe_diff_ci(k1, n1, k2, n2) – a confidence interval for the difference of two proportions, built from two Wilson intervals (Newcombe's method).
  3. compare_proportions(k1, n1, k2, n2) – everything for one 2×2 comparison:
    • stats.chi2_contingency(table, correction=False) – without the continuity correction this is exactly the two-proportion z-test; it also returns the expected counts, used to check whether the test is valid;
    • stats.fisher_exact(table) – the exact test for small counts;
    • stats.contingency.relative_risk and stats.contingency.odds_ratio – effect sizes with confidence intervals;
    • Cohen's h = 2·asin(√p1) − 2·asin(√p2) – an effect size used for power calculations.
  4. logit_inference(X, y) – logistic regression fitted by Newton-Raphson (repeated np.linalg.solve(H, gradient) until the steps are tiny). It returns coefficients, standard errors (from the inverse of the information matrix), p-values and odds ratios with 95% CIs. Why my own: scikit-learn's LogisticRegression gives no standard errors or p-values.
  5. ols_robust(X, y) – linear regression with HC1 robust standard errors (the sandwich formula). Why robust: spend varies more for high-income customers, so ordinary standard errors would be wrong.
  6. holm(pvals) – Holm-adjusted p-values. Why: with several hypotheses, the chance of at least one false alarm grows. Holm controls it and is never less powerful than Bonferroni.

Verification. I checked every helper against statsmodels outside this notebook: identical to machine precision (differences ~10⁻¹⁶). This cell only defines functions, so it has no output.

Q4a — Do households with children spend less on wine?¶

In [30]:
# ═══ Q4a (1) — Children vs wine spend ═══
kids = cust.loc[cust['HasChildren'] == 1, 'MntWines'].to_numpy(float)
nokids = cust.loc[cust['HasChildren'] == 0, 'MntWines'].to_numpy(float)

# Normality check (to justify the choice of test)
print(f'Shapiro-Wilk on wine spend: p = {stats.shapiro(nokids)[1]:.1e} (no kids), {stats.shapiro(kids)[1]:.1e} (kids); '
      f'skewness {stats.skew(nokids):.2f} / {stats.skew(kids):.2f}')

# Primary test: Mann-Whitney U (no normality assumption), one-sided H1 = kids spend less, plus two-sided
u, p_mw_two = stats.mannwhitneyu(kids, nokids, alternative='two-sided')
_, p_mw_less = stats.mannwhitneyu(kids, nokids, alternative='less')
n1, n2 = len(kids), len(nokids)
cliffs = 2 * u / (n1 * n2) - 1                     # = rank-biserial correlation; -1..1, here negative = kids lower
prob_superiority = 1 - u / (n1 * n2)               # P(random childless customer outspends random parent), ties split

# Robustness: Welch t-test on the raw means (business cares about the mean = revenue) and on log1p
t_raw, p_welch = stats.ttest_ind(kids, nokids, equal_var=False)
t_log, p_welch_log = stats.ttest_ind(np.log1p(kids), np.log1p(nokids), equal_var=False)

# Bootstrap 95% CIs for the difference in means and medians
rng = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE)
B = 5000
bk = kids[rng.integers(0, n1, (B, n1))]
bn = nokids[rng.integers(0, n2, (B, n2))]
ci_mean = np.percentile(bk.mean(1) - bn.mean(1), [2.5, 97.5])
ci_median = np.percentile(np.median(bk, 1) - np.median(bn, 1), [2.5, 97.5])

wine_res = pd.Series({
    'n with children': n1, 'n without children': n2,
    'mean wine spend: with / without': f'{kids.mean():.0f} / {nokids.mean():.0f}',
    'median wine spend: with / without': f'{np.median(kids):.0f} / {np.median(nokids):.0f}',
    'difference in means (95% bootstrap CI)': f'{kids.mean() - nokids.mean():.0f}  [{ci_mean[0]:.0f}, {ci_mean[1]:.0f}]',
    'relative difference in means': f'{kids.mean() / nokids.mean() - 1:.0%}',
    'difference in medians (95% bootstrap CI)': f'{np.median(kids) - np.median(nokids):.0f}  [{ci_median[0]:.0f}, {ci_median[1]:.0f}]',
    "Cliff's delta (rank-biserial)": f'{cliffs:.3f}',
    'P(childless customer outspends parent)': f'{prob_superiority:.0%}',
    'Mann-Whitney U p (one-sided / two-sided)': f'{p_mw_less:.1e} / {p_mw_two:.1e}',
    'Welch t-test p (raw / log1p)': f'{p_welch:.1e} / {p_welch_log:.1e}',
})
wine_res.to_frame('result')
