What I did – step by step

  1. Two arrays: kids (wine spend of the 1,434 households with children) and nokids (the 560 without).
  2. Checked normality first, to choose the test: stats.shapiro() and stats.skew().
  3. Main test: stats.mannwhitneyu(kids, nokids, alternative='two-sided'), plus alternative='less' for Marketing's directional claim.
  4. Effect size from the same test:
    • Cliff's δ = 2U / (n1·n2) − 1, from −1 to 1 – the effect size that belongs to Mann-Whitney;
    • the "probability of superiority", 1 − U / (n1·n2): the chance that a random childless customer out-spends a random parent.
  5. Robustness on the means: stats.ttest_ind(kids, nokids, equal_var=False) – Welch's t-test – on the raw values and on np.log1p values. Why also means: the business cares about averages, because revenue = mean × customers.
  6. Bootstrap 95% CIs: 5,000 resamples per group (rng.integers(0, n, (5000, n)), vectorised), the difference in means and medians for each, then the 2.5–97.5 percentiles.

Why these tests – and why I could use them here

  1. Shapiro-Wilk – tests "could this sample come from a normal distribution?". I use it only to choose the main test. Needs: independent observations ✓ and n ≤ 5,000 for scipy's version ✓ (560 and 1,434). Caveat: with large samples it flags even tiny deviations, so I also checked the skewness (0.44 and 1.60) – the non-normality is real, not a technicality.
  2. Mann-Whitney U (main test) – compares two groups using ranks instead of raw values. What it needs, and how this data meets it:
    • two independent groups – every customer is either "with children" or "without", never both, and the duplicates are gone ✓;
    • an outcome that can be ordered – wine spend ✓;
    • no normality ✓ – which is exactly why it beats the t-test here.
    • Read as "how often does one group out-spend the other", it is valid whatever the shape of the two distributions – and that is precisely what Cliff's δ reports.
    • Two-sided as the main test (it doesn't presume the direction); one-sided only for the directional claim "families spend less".
  3. Welch's t-test (robustness check on the means) – compares means without assuming equal variances. Needs: independent groups ✓; a roughly normal distribution of the sample mean – with 560 and 1,434 customers the central limit theorem delivers this even for skewed spend ✓. The ordinary Student t-test would also require equal variances, which fails here: the standard deviations are 291 (with children) vs 368 (without), a variance ratio of 1.6. Welch does not need them equal.
  4. Bootstrap confidence intervals – resample customers with replacement and recompute the statistic. Needs only independent customers ✓ and groups large enough to represent their population ✓. No formula and no normality – and it works for the median, for which no simple CI formula exists.

Output and what it means.

  • Shapiro-Wilk p = 2.5·10⁻¹² and 3.3·10⁻⁴⁰; skewness 0.44 and 1.60 → far from normal, so Mann-Whitney is the right primary test.
  • Mean wine spend 232 vs 500 (−54%), difference −268 (95% CI −301 to −235); median 97 vs 466.
  • Cliff's δ = −0.44: a random childless customer out-spends a random parent on wine 72% of the time.
  • Mann-Whitney p ≈ 10⁻⁵¹; Welch confirms (p ≈ 10⁻⁴⁷).

The claim is true, and the effect is large.

How to read the numbers

  • Shapiro-Wilk p – below 0.05 = "not normal". Both values are astronomically small → clearly not normal.
  • Skewness – 0 = symmetric; 0.5–1 = moderately and above 1 = strongly right-skewed (a long tail of big spenders). 1.60 for parents → strongly skewed.
  • Mann-Whitney p ≈ 9·10⁻⁵² – the probability of a rank difference this big if parents and non-parents spent the same on wine: practically zero.
  • Cliff's δ – from −1 to +1: P(random parent spends more) − P(random non-parent spends more). 0 = no difference, −1 = every non-parent out-spends every parent. Thresholds: |δ| < 0.15 negligible, 0.15–0.33 small, 0.33–0.47 medium, ≥ 0.47 large. −0.44 = medium, just short of large.
  • Probability of superiority 72% – the same thing in plain words: pick one random childless customer and one random parent; 72% of the time the childless one spent more on wine. 50% would mean no difference.
  • 95% CI −301 to −235 – the range of plausible values for the true difference in mean wine spend. It does not contain 0 → the difference is real; even its most optimistic end is a 235 gap.
  • Welch p – read like the Mann-Whitney p; it confirms the result on the means.

What I did – step by step

  1. lab = cust[cust['Response'].notna()] – only the 1,975 customers with a trustworthy label.
  2. compare_proportions() on two outcomes: the latest campaign (Response), and "accepted any of the 6 campaigns" (earlier acceptances + Response > 0), so the conclusion doesn't depend on a single campaign.
  3. holm() across the three tests of Marketing's claims (wine, latest campaign, any campaign).

Why these tests – and why I could use them here

  • Chi-square test of independence on the 2×2 table (children yes/no × responded yes/no) – the standard test for "do two proportions differ?". What it needs, and how this data meets it:
    • independent customers, each counted in exactly one cell ✓;
    • at least 5 expected customers in every cell – the smallest expected count is 82 ✓ (151 for "any campaign");
    • only the 1,975 labelled customers – an unknown label can't be put in a cell.
    • Without the continuity correction it is identical to the two-proportion z-test. With counts this large the correction isn't needed; it would only make the test overly cautious.
  • Fisher's exact test is reported alongside: it has no sample-size requirement, and it agrees.
  • Confidence intervals for the relative risk and odds ratio (scipy.stats.contingency) are large-sample intervals on the log scale, which need reasonably large cell counts – every cell here has more than 130 customers ✓.
  • Holm correction – I tested three hypotheses about families. Each extra test adds a chance of a false alarm. Holm keeps the overall false-alarm rate at 5% and is valid whatever the dependence between the tests – essential here, because all three use the same customers (the Šidák or Hochberg corrections would assume independent or positively related tests).

Output and what it means.

  • Latest campaign: 9.6% vs 27.8%, a difference of −18.2 points (95% CI −22.4 to −14.3). Relative risk 0.34 (about three times less likely), odds ratio 0.28, Cohen's h −0.48. The smallest expected count is 82, so the chi-square test is valid.
  • Any of the 6 campaigns: 19.8% vs 45.8% (−26 points).
  • After the Holm correction, all three tests remain highly significant (adjusted p < 10⁻²⁴).

How to read the numbers

  • diff_pp −18.2 (95% CI −22.4 to −14.3) – a difference in percentage points. The interval excludes 0 → significant; the true gap is at least 14 points.
  • Relative risk 0.34 (0.28–0.42) – parents respond at 34% of the rate of non-parents, i.e. about 3× less often. 1 = no difference.
  • Odds ratio 0.28 (0.21–0.36) – the same comparison on the odds scale (odds = p / (1 − p)). 1 = no difference. When the outcome is common (28% here) the odds ratio looks more extreme than the relative risk, so for communication use the relative risk. I report the odds ratio because logistic regression (next cell) speaks in odds ratios.
  • Cohen's h = −0.48 – a standardised difference between two proportions: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large → medium.
  • min_expected_count 82 – the validity check of the chi-square test (needs ≥ 5).
  • p_chi2 / p_fisher shown as 0.0 – smaller than the display precision; the Holm table shows the real size (10⁻²⁵ to 10⁻³¹).
  • Holm-adjusted p – a p-value already corrected for testing three hypotheses; compare it with 0.05 as usual.

# Is it really the CHILDREN, or just lower income / age? And is it young kids or teenagers?
print('Mean income: with children {:,.0f} vs without {:,.0f}'.format(*cust.groupby('HasChildren')['Income'].mean()[[1, 0]]))

def income_controls(frame, spec):
    if spec == 'log income (linear)':
        return pd.DataFrame({'log_income': np.log(frame['Income'])}, index=frame.index)
    deciles = pd.qcut(cust['Income'], 10, labels=False).loc[frame.index]     # same cut points for both outcomes
    return pd.get_dummies(deciles, prefix='inc_decile', drop_first=True).astype(float)

rows = []
for outcome, frame in [('Wine spend (log1p)', cust), ('Response (latest campaign)', lab)]:
    for spec in ['log income (linear)', 'income deciles (flexible)']:
        for terms in (['HasChildren'], ['Kidhome', 'Teenhome']):
            X = pd.concat([frame[terms].astype(float), frame[['Age']].div(10).rename(columns={'Age': 'Age_10y'}),
                           income_controls(frame, spec)], axis=1)
            res = (ols_robust(X, np.log1p(frame['MntWines'])) if outcome.startswith('Wine')
                   else logit_inference(X, frame['Response']))
            for t in terms:
                b, se, p = res.loc[t, ['coef', 'se', 'p_value']]
                lo, hi = b - Z975 * se, b + Z975 * se
                if outcome.startswith('Wine'):     # report as % change in wine spend at equal income & age
                    eff, ci = f'{np.exp(b) - 1:+.0%}', f'{np.exp(lo) - 1:+.0%} to {np.exp(hi) - 1:+.0%}'
                else:                              # report as odds ratio
                    eff, ci = f'OR {np.exp(b):.2f}', f'{np.exp(lo):.2f} to {np.exp(hi):.2f}'
                rows.append({'outcome': outcome, 'income control': spec, 'term': t, 'adjusted effect': eff,
                             '95% CI': ci, 'p_value': f'{p:.1e}'})
adjusted = pd.DataFrame(rows)
adjusted

What I did – step by step. Parents earn less (mean income 46k vs 66k), and income drives both spend and response. So I re-estimated both effects at equal income and age:

  1. Wine: ols_robust(X, np.log1p(MntWines)). log1p handles the skew and the zeros; the coefficient becomes a % effect via exp(b) − 1.

  2. Response: logit_inference(X, Response), reported as an odds ratio, exp(b).

  3. X = the children term(s) + age (in decades) + income, with income entered two ways:

    • np.log(Income) – a straight-line effect;
    • pd.get_dummies(pd.qcut(Income, 10), drop_first=True) – 9 income-decile dummies that assume no shape at all.

    Why two ways: if the conclusion holds under both, it doesn't depend on how I modelled income.

  4. Two versions of the children term: HasChildren (0/1), then Kidhome and Teenhome separately (number of young kids / teenagers at home) – to see which children matter.

  5. The confidence interval for each effect: coefficient ± 1.96 × standard error, converted to % or to an odds ratio.

Why regression – and why I could use these two models here

  • Why a model at all: a two-group test can't separate "has children" from "earns less". A regression estimates the children effect while holding income and age fixed.
  • Linear regression (OLS) with HC1 robust standard errors on log1p(wine spend). What it needs, and how this data meets it:
    • an outcome that is roughly symmetric – log1p turns the skewed, zero-containing spend into one ✓;
    • independent customers ✓;
    • predictors that aren't strongly correlated with each other – VIF ≤ 1.29 ✓ (Appendix);
    • equal error variance – not needed: HC1 standard errors stay valid when the spread differs between customers, which it does (richer customers vary more);
    • normal errors – not needed for the confidence intervals with 1,994 customers (central limit theorem).
  • Logistic regression (fitted by maximum likelihood, Newton-Raphson) for the 0/1 response. What it needs:
    • a binary outcome ✓ and independent customers ✓;
    • log-odds that change linearly with continuous predictors – for income I don't rely on this: once as log(income), once as 9 deciles with no shape at all, same answer ✓;
    • enough events per parameter (≥ 10) – 26 to 97 ✓ (Appendix), so the unpenalised estimates and their confidence intervals are reliable;
    • no strong collinearity ✓.

Output and what it means.

  • Wine, at equal income: HasChildren alone is only −11% to −15%, so most of the raw −54% gap is income. Split up: each young child −38% to −52% under both specifications; teenagers: no reduction (+4% to +19%).
  • Response, at equal income: HasChildren odds ratio 0.33–0.40. Split up: teenagers 0.34–0.41 (robust); young kids ≈ 0.9, not significant.
  • So the two claims have different causes: wine is about young children, responsiveness is about teenagers.

How to read the numbers

  • % effect (wine) = exp(b) − 1: how much more or less wine a household buys compared with an otherwise identical household (same income and age). For HasChildren it compares with vs without children; for Kidhome / Teenhome it is per additional young child / teenager. −52% = about half the wine spend.
  • Odds ratio (response) = exp(b): 1 = no effect; 0.34 = the odds of accepting are about one third.
  • The confidence interval decides: if it contains 0% (or an odds ratio of 1), the effect can't be told apart from no effect. Teenagers on wine in the flexible model: +4% (−5% to +13%) → contains 0 → no effect. Young kids on response: OR 0.89 (0.65–1.22) → contains 1 → no effect.
  • p – below 0.05 = significant (e.g. Teenhome on response 2·10⁻⁸ in the flexible model).
  • "Log income" vs "income deciles" – two ways of holding income fixed. When both rows tell the same story, the conclusion doesn't depend on that modelling choice.

    a = g.loc[g.HasChildren == 1, 'Response'].sum(); b_ = (g.HasChildren == 1).sum() - a
    c = g.loc[g.HasChildren == 0, 'Response'].sum(); d = (g.HasChildren == 0).sum() - c
    tables.append(np.array([[a, b_], [c, d]], float))
num = sum(t[0, 0] - t[0].sum() * t[:, 0].sum() / t.sum() for t in tables)
var = sum(t[0].sum() * t[1].sum() * t[:, 0].sum() * t[:, 1].sum() / (t.sum() ** 2 * (t.sum() - 1)) for t in tables)
cmh = (abs(num) - 0.5) ** 2 / var
mh_or = sum(t[0, 0] * t[1, 1] / t.sum() for t in tables) / sum(t[0, 1] * t[1, 0] / t.sum() for t in tables)
print(f'Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (stratified by income quartile): chi2 = {cmh:.1f}, p = {stats.chi2.sf(cmh, 1):.1e}, '
      f'Mantel-Haenszel common odds ratio = {mh_or:.2f}')
strat.style.format({('mean', 0): '{:.1%}', ('mean', 1): '{:.1%}'})

Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (stratified by income quartile): chi2 = 39.8, p = 2.9e-10, Mantel-Haenszel common odds ratio = 0.35

What I did – step by step

  1. lab.groupby(['IncomeQuartile', 'HasChildren'])['Response'].agg(['mean', 'size']).unstack() – response rates for families vs non-families side by side within each income quartile. A table a stakeholder can read.
  2. A 2×2 table per quartile (children × responded), and from those the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel statistic and the Mantel-Haenszel common odds ratio, computed directly from the formula.

Why the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test – and why I could use it here

  • The question: "do families respond less within the same income band?". CMH combines the 2×2 tables of all income quartiles into one test, so the income gap between families and non-families can't produce the effect. It is the classic, assumption-light stratified test – a transparent complement to the logistic regression in the previous cell.
  • What it needs, and how this data meets it:
    • independent customers ✓;
    • strata defined in advance – income quartiles ✓;
    • enough customers in total – the CMH χ² is reliable when the summed counts are large, not each cell (1,975 customers; the smallest stratum group has 43) ✓.
  • One extra condition for the summary number: the test itself is valid even if the effect differs between bands, but the single common odds ratio (0.35) is a fair summary only if the bands agree (homogeneity). I tested this in the Appendix with a likelihood-ratio test: p = 0.007 → they don't agree, so I report the effect band by band.

Output and what it means.

  • In the top three quartiles, childless customers respond 2–3.5× more – e.g. the top quartile 34.7% vs 10.5%.
  • In the lowest quartile there is no gap (9.5% vs 10.2%).
  • CMH: χ² = 39.8, p ≈ 3·10⁻¹⁰, common odds ratio 0.35.

Because the effect is not the same in every band, the pooled 0.35 is an average of "no effect at the bottom" and a strong effect everywhere else. I report the effect per band.

How to read the numbers

  • Rate table – read across one row: same income band, families vs non-families. E.g. Q4: 34.7% vs 10.5% → childless customers respond 3.3× more often. The size columns show how many customers each rate is based on (Q2 non-families: only 43 → that rate is less precise).
  • CMH χ² = 39.8 (1 degree of freedom) – if families and non-families responded equally within every band, values above 3.84 would occur only 5% of the time. 39.8 → p = 3·10⁻¹⁰ → the within-band difference is real.
  • Common odds ratio 0.35 – the average within-band odds ratio; 1 = no effect. It is only a fair average when the bands agree – here they don't (1.08 in Q1 vs 0.22–0.38 elsewhere).

Q4b — Are complainers less likely to respond?¶

      f'non-complainers: {k2}/{n2} ({k2/n2:.1%})')

What I did – step by step

  1. Counts: 19 labelled complainers, of whom 3 responded; 1,956 non-complainers, of whom 288 responded.
  2. compare_proportions(3, 19, 288, 1956) – all tests and effect sizes in one call.
  3. wilson_ci(3, 19) – a confidence interval that works for a group this small.
  4. The expected number of responders if complainers behaved like everyone else: 19 × 288 / 1,956.

Why Fisher's exact test – and why I could use it here

  • The chi-square test needs at least 5 expected customers per cell. Here only 2.8 responders are expected among complainers → the chi-square p-value (0.90) can't be trusted.
  • Fisher's exact test computes the p-value exactly, by enumerating every possible table with the same row and column totals – no sample-size requirement. It needs only independent customers ✓ and a fixed 2×2 classification ✓. It is slightly conservative (p a little too large), which is acceptable.
  • Wilson interval instead of the textbook p ± 1.96·SE: with 3 of 19 the textbook interval would be −0.6% to 32% – a negative response rate is impossible. Wilson stays inside 0–100% and is accurate for small groups.
  • Newcombe interval for the difference – built from two Wilson intervals, so it is also valid for small groups.

Output and what it means.

  • 15.8% vs 14.7% – complainers even respond slightly more, but the 95% CI for the difference is −9.3 to +22.9 points.
  • Only 2.8 responders are expected among complainers, so the chi-square test is invalid. Fisher's exact test: p = 0.75.
  • Wilson CI for the complainers alone: 5.5%–37.6% – a huge range.

There is no evidence of an effect – but the next cell shows whether the test could even detect one.

How to read the numbers

  • Fisher p = 0.75 – a difference like this (or a bigger one) appears 75% of the time by pure chance → no evidence of any effect.
  • CI of the difference −9.3 to +22.9 points – contains 0, and it is very wide: complainers could respond 9 points less or 23 points more. The data can't tell.
  • Wilson CI 5.5%–37.6% – the plausible range of the complainers' true response rate.
  • Relative risk 1.07 (0.38–3.05) – anything from "less than half as likely" to "three times as likely" fits the data.
  • min_expected_count 2.8 – the validity check that fails (needs ≥ 5), which is why Fisher is the test to read.
In [35]:
# How much power does a test with n1 complainers have?
p0, alpha = k2 / n2, 0.05

def power_two_prop(p1, p2, n1, n2, alpha=0.05):
    """Normal-approximation power (arcsine / Cohen's h), two-sided."""
    h = abs(2 * np.arcsin(np.sqrt(p1)) - 2 * np.arcsin(np.sqrt(p2)))
    return stats.norm.sf(stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2) - h / np.sqrt(1 / n1 + 1 / n2))

def simulated_power_fisher(p1, p2, n1, n2, sims=4000, seed=RANDOM_STATE):
    """Exact-test power by simulation (more honest than the normal approximation for n1 = 19)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x1, x2 = rng.binomial(n1, p1, sims), rng.binomial(n2, p2, sims)
    return np.mean([stats.fisher_exact([[a, n1 - a], [b, n2 - b]])[1] < alpha for a, b in zip(x1, x2)])

scen = pd.DataFrame({'true_rate_complainers': [0.0, p0 / 4, p0 / 2, 0.75 * p0, p0 * 1.5, p0 * 2]})
scen['relative_change'] = scen['true_rate_complainers'] / p0 - 1
scen['power_normal_approx'] = [power_two_prop(p, p0, n1, n2) for p in scen['true_rate_complainers']]
scen['power_fisher_simulated'] = [simulated_power_fisher(p, p0, n1, n2) for p in scen['true_rate_complainers']]

# Minimum detectable effect at 80% power with the current group sizes
h_mde = (stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2) + stats.norm.ppf(0.8)) * np.sqrt(1 / n1 + 1 / n2)
mde_low = np.sin(np.arcsin(np.sqrt(p0)) - h_mde / 2) ** 2
mde_high = np.sin(np.arcsin(np.sqrt(p0)) + h_mde / 2) ** 2

# Complainers needed (non-complainer group fixed) to detect a halving of the response rate with 80% power
h_half = 2 * np.arcsin(np.sqrt(p0)) - 2 * np.arcsin(np.sqrt(p0 / 2))
need = 1 / ((h_half / (stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2) + stats.norm.ppf(0.8))) ** 2 - 1 / n2)
complaint_rate = cust['Complain'].mean()
print(f'Minimum detectable effect (80% power, alpha 5%): complainers would need a response rate below {mde_low:.1%} '
      f'or above {mde_high:.1%} (vs {p0:.1%}).')
print(f'To detect a halving ({p0:.1%} -> {p0/2:.1%}) we need ~{need:.0f} complainers (we have {n1}); '
      f'at a {complaint_rate:.1%} complaint rate that is a base of ~{need / complaint_rate:,.0f} customers.')
best_case_p = stats.fisher_exact([[0, n1], [k2, n2 - k2]])[1]
print(f'Best possible case for the hypothesis - NOT ONE of the {n1} complainers responds: Fisher two-sided p = {best_case_p:.3f} '
      f'(one-sided p = {stats.fisher_exact([[0, n1], [k2, n2 - k2]], alternative="less")[1]:.3f})')
scen.style.format({'true_rate_complainers': '{:.1%}', 'relative_change': '{:+.0%}', 'power_normal_approx': '{:.0%}',
                   'power_fisher_simulated': '{:.0%}'})

Minimum detectable effect (80% power, alpha 5%): complainers would need a response rate below 0.5% or above 43.2% (vs 14.7%).
To detect a halving (14.7% -> 7.4%) we need ~149 complainers (we have 19); at a 1.0% complaint rate that is a base of ~15,638 customers.
Best possible case for the hypothesis - NOT ONE of the 19 complainers responds: Fisher two-sided p = 0.096 (one-sided p = 0.049)

  true_rate_complainers relative_change power_normal_approx power_fisher_simulated
0 0.0% -100% 93% 0%
1 3.7% -75% 41% 0%
2 7.4% -50% 18% 0%
3 11.0% -25% 7% 1%
4 22.1% +50% 13% 17%
5 29.4% +100% 34% 40%

What I did – step by step

  1. Power from the formula: power_two_prop() – the normal approximation using Cohen's h.
  2. Power by simulation: simulated_power_fisher() uses rng.binomial to generate 4,000 fake datasets for each assumed true response rate of complainers (0%, 3.7%, 7.4%, 11%, 22%, 29%), runs fisher_exact on each, and counts how often p < 0.05.
  3. Minimum detectable effect at 80% power and 5% significance, and the number of complainers needed to detect a halving – both from the Cohen's h formula.
  4. The best case for the hypothesis: stats.fisher_exact([[0, 19], [288, 1668]]) – the p-value if none of the 19 had responded.

Why a power analysis – and why simulation

  • A non-significant result has two possible meanings: "there is no effect" or "the test is too weak to see one". Power tells them apart: it is the probability that the test detects an effect of a given size if that effect really exists. The usual target is 80%.
  • The formula (normal approximation) assumes large samples – several expected events per group. That fails here (2.8 expected), so I show it only to demonstrate how wrong it gets.
  • The simulation generates thousands of datasets from a binomial model (every customer responds independently with a given probability – the same assumption as every test above ✓) and runs the test I actually use (Fisher) on each. It is valid at any sample size, so this is the number to trust.

Output and what it means.

  • Best case: even with 0 of 19 responding, two-sided p = 0.096 (not significant), so the test cannot ever confirm "complainers respond less".
  • Simulated power to detect any reduction is 0%. The formula claims up to 93% – a good illustration of why approximations fail with ~3 expected events.
  • Detectable at 80% power: only rates below 0.5% or above 43%.
  • Detecting a halving (14.7% → 7.4%) needs ~149 complainers (we have 19) – a customer base of ~15,600 at the current 1% complaint rate.

How to read the numbers

  • Power 0% – even if complainers truly never responded, the test would (almost) never reach p < 0.05. A test with 0% power can't confirm the claim whatever the truth is – so "not significant" here means "we can't know", not "no effect".
  • power_normal_approx vs power_fisher_simulated – the same question answered by the formula and by simulation; when they disagree this much, the formula's assumptions are broken.
  • Minimum detectable effect – the smallest true difference the test would catch 80% of the time: here only rates below 0.5% or above 43% (vs 14.7%).
  • 149 complainers – the sample needed for a halving to be detected with 80% power.
In [36]:
# Bayesian view (Beta(1,1) priors): what we actually know about the two rates
rng = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE)
post_c = rng.beta(1 + k1, 1 + n1 - k1, 200_000)
post_n = rng.beta(1 + k2, 1 + n2 - k2, 200_000)
diff = post_c - post_n
print(f'P(complainers respond LESS than non-complainers | data) = {(diff < 0).mean():.0%}')
print(f'95% credible interval for the difference: {np.percentile(diff, 2.5):+.1%} to {np.percentile(diff, 97.5):+.1%}')
print(f'P(difference is "material", i.e. more than 5 pp lower) = {(diff < -0.05).mean():.0%}')

P(complainers respond LESS than non-complainers | data) = 34%
95% credible interval for the difference: -9.2% to +23.2%
P(difference is "material", i.e. more than 5 pp lower) = 13%

What I did. A Bayesian view of what the data does tell us:

  • rng.beta(1 + k, 1 + n − k, 200_000) draws 200,000 plausible values of each group's response rate – the Beta posterior with a flat Beta(1, 1) prior;
  • the difference between the two sets of draws gives the probability that complainers respond less, and a 95% credible interval.

Why a Bayesian Beta-Binomial model – and why I could use it here

  • It answers the question a stakeholder actually asks – "how likely is it that complainers respond less?" – which a p-value does not.
  • What it assumes: within each group, every customer responds independently with the same probability (binomial) ✓; the prior Beta(1, 1) says every rate from 0% to 100% is equally plausible beforehand – no opinion injected. With this prior the posterior is exact – Beta(1 + responders, 1 + non-responders) – with no large-sample approximation, so it is valid even with 19 customers.

Output and what it means.

  • P(complainers respond less) = 34%.
  • 95% credible interval for the difference: −9% to +23%.
  • P(more than 5 points lower) = 13%.

In plain words: we know almost nothing either way. Advice:

  • track complainers over the next campaigns;
  • use all six campaigns per customer;
  • sharpen the question – did the complaint come before or after the offer?
  • meanwhile, don't send promotions to customers with an open complaint.

How to read the numbers

  • P(complainers respond less) = 34% – 50% would be a coin flip; to act on a claim you'd want 90–95% or more. 34% means the data leans slightly the other way – and only weakly.
  • 95% credible interval −9% to +23% – given the data, there is a 95% probability that the true difference lies in this range (unlike a confidence interval, it can be read this way directly). It contains 0 and is wide → we don't know.
  • P(more than 5 points lower) = 13% – a material reduction is unlikely, but not ruled out.

Q4c — A/B test design: "free delivery over $30"¶

In [37]:
# ═══ Q4c — A/B test design: numbers from the data ═══
# Two numbers from this data that shape the design (MU treated as $ for illustration)
aov = cust['AvgSpendPerOrder']
monthly_spend = cust['MntTotal'] / 24
print(f'Customers whose average order is already >= 30: {(aov >= 30).mean():.0%} '
      f'(median average order = {aov.median():.1f}) -> they get free delivery without changing behaviour')
print(f'Customers with an average order between 20 and 30 (the "nudgeable" zone): {aov.between(20, 30, inclusive="left").mean():.0%}')

def n_per_arm_prop(p_base, mde_abs, alpha=0.05, power=0.8):
    p2 = p_base + mde_abs
    z = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2) + stats.norm.ppf(power)
    return int(np.ceil(z ** 2 * (p_base * (1 - p_base) + p2 * (1 - p2)) / mde_abs ** 2))

def n_per_arm_mean(sd, mde_abs, alpha=0.05, power=0.8):
    z = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2) + stats.norm.ppf(power)
    return int(np.ceil(2 * (z * sd / mde_abs) ** 2))

sd_m, mean_m = monthly_spend.std(), monthly_spend.mean()
ss = pd.DataFrame([
    {'metric': 'Order conversion in test window', 'baseline': '15%', 'MDE': '+1.5 pp (10% relative)', 'n_per_arm': n_per_arm_prop(0.15, 0.015)},
    {'metric': 'Order conversion in test window', 'baseline': '15%', 'MDE': '+0.75 pp (5% relative)', 'n_per_arm': n_per_arm_prop(0.15, 0.0075)},
    {'metric': 'Net revenue per customer / month', 'baseline': f'{mean_m:.1f} (sd {sd_m:.1f})', 'MDE': f'+{0.05 * mean_m:.2f} (5% relative)',
     'n_per_arm': n_per_arm_mean(sd_m, 0.05 * mean_m)},
    {'metric': '  ... same with CUPED (pre-period corr. 0.7)', 'baseline': '', 'MDE': f'+{0.05 * mean_m:.2f} (5% relative)',
     'n_per_arm': n_per_arm_mean(sd_m * np.sqrt(1 - 0.7 ** 2), 0.05 * mean_m)},
])
ss.style.format({'n_per_arm': '{:,}'}).hide(axis='index')

Customers whose average order is already >= 30: 50% (median average order = 29.9) -> they get free delivery without changing behaviour
Customers with an average order between 20 and 30 (the "nudgeable" zone): 15%
Out[37]:
metric baseline MDE n_per_arm
Order conversion in test window 15% +1.5 pp (10% relative) 9,254
Order conversion in test window 15% +0.75 pp (5% relative) 36,307
Net revenue per customer / month 25.3 (sd 25.1) +1.27 (5% relative) 6,139
... same with CUPED (pre-period corr. 0.7) +1.27 (5% relative) 3,131

What I did – the numbers behind the design

  1. (AvgSpendPerOrder >= 30).mean() – how many customers already average $30+ per order; .between(20, 30) – how many sit just below the threshold.

  2. Sample size: n_per_arm_mean() implements n = 2·(z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈)²·σ² / δ² – 5% significance, 80% power.

    • σ = the standard deviation of monthly spend (MntTotal / 24);
    • δ = a 5% change;
    • CUPED (adjusting for each customer's pre-test spend) multiplies σ by √(1 − ρ²), with an assumed correlation ρ = 0.7.

    n_per_arm_prop() does the same for a conversion metric.

Why this sample-size formula – and why I could use it

  • It is the sample size of a two-sample z-test on means: 5% false-alarm rate (two-sided) and 80% power. It assumes that the average of each group is approximately normal – true with thousands of customers per group by the central limit theorem, even though individual spend is skewed ✓ – and that customers are independent, which randomising by customer guarantees ✓.
  • σ is estimated from this data (monthly spend SD 25.1), so the numbers reflect iFood's real variability.
  • CUPED assumes that pre-period and test-period spend are correlated. ρ = 0.7 is an assumption that has to be measured in the A/A test before launch.
  • The conversion version uses the two-proportion z-test with the same logic.

Output and what it means.

  • 50% of customers already average $30+ per order (median 29.9). For them the offer is pure cost – they get free delivery without changing anything. Only **15%** sit in the "nudgeable" $20–30 zone.
  • Monthly spend averages 25.3 (SD 25.1). Detecting +5% needs ~6,100 customers per arm, or ~3,100 with CUPED. A conversion metric would need 9,300–36,300 per arm.

How to read the numbers

  • MDE (minimum detectable effect) – the smallest true change the test will catch 80% of the time; here +5% = +1.27 per customer per month.
  • n_per_arm – customers needed in each group (control and treatment). 6,139 → ~12,300 in total; with CUPED 3,131 → the same precision with half the customers.
  • Power 80% / significance 5% – a real +5% effect is missed 20% of the time; an effect that doesn't exist is "found" 5% of the time.

The design

  • Hypotheses: H0 – no change in contribution margin per customer; H1 – a change. The test is two-sided, because the offer can also lose money.
  • Randomisation: by customer – not by session or order – using a hash of the customer ID, so a customer always sees the same version. Stratified by segment and region, 50/50, with an A/A test and sample-ratio checks first.
  • Primary metric: contribution margin per customer (revenue − product cost − delivery subsidy − discounts). Conversion alone would reward an offer that sells more and earns less.
  • Guardrails: delivery time, delivery cost per order, cancellations, complaints, unsubscribes, "basket padding" just above $30, and retention after the test.
  • Duration: at least two full weeks (weekday and weekend patterns), and no peeking at results.
  • What could invalidate it:
    • shared courier capacity – more orders in treatment slow down deliveries for the control group too;
    • contamination through shared accounts and promo codes;
    • novelty effects and orders pulled forward in time;
    • seasonality.

Conclusions – Q4

  • Both of Marketing's claims hold, and the effects are large: households with children spend 54% less on wine and respond about 3× less often (9.6% vs 27.8%).
  • The causes differ. The wine gap comes mostly from income and young children; the response gap comes from households with teenagers, and it disappears in the lowest income band.
  • The complaint question can't be answered with this data: with 19 complainers, not even a zero response rate would be statistically convincing. The result is inconclusive, not "no effect".
  • The free-delivery A/B test should randomise customers, measure margin per customer, run at least 2 weeks with ~3,000–6,000 customers per group, and watch delivery times.

In plain words for Marketing:

  • Treat "young-kid families" and "teen families" as two different audiences: the first buys less wine, the second ignores campaigns.
  • Don't draw conclusions about complainers yet.
  • Judge the free-delivery offer on profit – half of customers already order above $30 and would get it for free.

Q5 — Predictive model: who will respond to the next campaign?¶

Task: build a model, evaluate it properly for an imbalanced target, explain the top drivers, and flag the risks.

Features, leakage and the split¶

    ('TotalChildren, HasChildren, TotalPurchases, ChannelPurchases', 'linear combinations of columns already included'),
    ('marital_* / education_* dummies', 'replaced by the collapsed categorical columns (one-hot encoded inside the pipeline)'),
    ('Customer_Days, TenureYears_asReported, EnrolDate', 'same information as TenureYears (a constant shift)'),
    ('ResponseConflict rows (19)', 'label unknown - cannot be used for training or evaluation'),
], columns=['excluded', 'why'])
display(excluded)

model_df = cust[cust['Response'].notna()].copy()
X = model_df[FEATURES].copy()
X[CAT_FEATURES] = X[CAT_FEATURES].astype(str)
y = model_df['Response'].astype(int)

# 80/20 stratified split. The test set is touched ONCE, at the very end.
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
print(f'{len(FEATURES)} input columns | train {len(X_train):,} rows ({y_train.mean():.1%} positive, {y_train.sum()} responders) | '
      f'test {len(X_test):,} rows ({y_test.mean():.1%} positive, {y_test.sum()} responders)')

What I did – step by step

  1. Imported the scikit-learn building blocks: splitting and cross-validation, pipelines, preprocessing, the three model types, and the metrics.
  2. Explicit feature lists, so every model gets exactly the same inputs:
    • LOG_FEATURES – the 6 spend columns + AvgSpendPerOrder, which will be log-transformed;
    • NUM_FEATURES – income, age, kids, teens, tenure, recency, purchase counts, web visits, complaint flag and the 5 earlier-campaign flags;
    • CAT_FEATURES – education and marital status.
  3. The excluded-features table, so every exclusion is documented:
    • the target itself;
    • the constant Z_ columns;
    • exact sums of columns already included (AcceptedCmpOverall, MntTotal, TotalChildren, …) – they would duplicate information and destabilise the coefficients;
    • the raw dummies, replaced by the categorical columns;
    • the 19 unknown labels.
  4. model_df = cust[cust['Response'].notna()] – the labelled customers only.
  5. train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42). Why stratify=y: with only 15% responders, a purely random split could leave the test set with noticeably more or fewer responders, and every metric would shift. Stratifying keeps the same share in both.

Output and what it means. 26 input columns; 1,580 training customers (233 responders) and 395 test customers (58 responders), 14.7% in both. The test set is used once, at the very end.

Candidate models¶

In [39]:
# ═══ Q5 — Pipelines, models, search spaces ═══
CAT_LEVELS = {'Education': EDU_ORDER, 'Marital_Status': MARITAL_ORDER}
CAT_REF = {'Education': 'Graduation', 'Marital_Status': 'Married'}

def make_preprocessor(log_cols=LOG_FEATURES, num_cols=NUM_FEATURES, cat_cols=CAT_FEATURES):
    """All preprocessing lives inside the pipeline, so it is re-fitted on each CV training fold (no leakage)."""
    return ColumnTransformer([
        ('log', Pipeline([('impute', SimpleImputer(strategy='median')),
                          ('log1p', FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out='one-to-one')),
                          ('scale', StandardScaler())]), log_cols),
        ('num', Pipeline([('impute', SimpleImputer(strategy='median')), ('scale', StandardScaler())]), num_cols),
        # explicit reference levels (most common) -> each coefficient reads "vs. Graduation" / "vs. Married"
        ('cat', OneHotEncoder(categories=[CAT_LEVELS[c] for c in cat_cols], drop=[CAT_REF[c] for c in cat_cols],
                              sparse_output=False), cat_cols),
    ], verbose_feature_names_out=False)

def make_logreg(**kw):
    # scikit-learn >= 1.8 sets the penalty through l1_ratio (0 = L2, 1 = L1); older versions need penalty='elasticnet'
    extra = {} if SK_VERSION >= (1, 8) else {'penalty': 'elasticnet'}
    return LogisticRegression(solver='saga', max_iter=20_000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, **extra, **kw)

pipes = {
    'Baseline (always predict the base rate)': Pipeline([('prep', make_preprocessor()), ('clf', DummyClassifier(strategy='prior'))]),
    'Logistic regression': Pipeline([('prep', make_preprocessor()), ('clf', make_logreg())]),
    'Random forest': Pipeline([('prep', make_preprocessor()), ('clf', RandomForestClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1))]),
    'Gradient boosting': Pipeline([('prep', make_preprocessor()), ('clf', HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE))]),
}
spaces = {
    'Logistic regression': {'clf__C': np.logspace(-3, 2, 11), 'clf__l1_ratio': [0.0, 0.5, 1.0],
                            'clf__class_weight': [None, 'balanced']},                                   # grid search: 66 combos
    'Random forest': {'clf__n_estimators': [300, 600], 'clf__max_depth': [None, 4, 6, 8, 12],
                      'clf__min_samples_leaf': randint(1, 30), 'clf__max_features': ['sqrt', 0.3, 0.5],
                      'clf__class_weight': [None, 'balanced_subsample']},                               # random search
    'Gradient boosting': {'clf__learning_rate': loguniform(0.01, 0.3), 'clf__max_iter': randint(100, 600),
                          'clf__max_leaf_nodes': randint(4, 40), 'clf__min_samples_leaf': randint(10, 80),
                          'clf__l2_regularization': loguniform(1e-3, 10), 'clf__class_weight': [None, 'balanced']},
}
SCORING = {'AP': 'average_precision', 'ROC_AUC': 'roc_auc', 'Brier': 'neg_brier_score'}

def make_search(name, cv, n_iter=30):
    if name == 'Logistic regression':
        return GridSearchCV(pipes[name], spaces[name], scoring=SCORING, refit='AP', cv=cv, n_jobs=-1)
    return RandomizedSearchCV(pipes[name], spaces[name], n_iter=n_iter, scoring=SCORING, refit='AP', cv=cv,
                              n_jobs=-1, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

What I did – step by step

  1. make_preprocessor() – a ColumnTransformer that sends each group of columns through its own Pipeline:
    • spend: SimpleImputer(strategy='median') → FunctionTransformer(np.log1p) → StandardScaler(). log1p = log(1 + x) compresses the skewed amounts and handles zeros; StandardScaler gives every feature mean 0 and SD 1, which a regularised logistic regression needs so that its penalty treats all features equally;
    • other numbers: median imputation → scaling;
    • categories: OneHotEncoder(categories=[...], drop=['Graduation', 'Married']). Why drop explicit reference levels: each coefficient then reads "vs. Graduation" or "vs. Married", and dropping one level per variable avoids perfect collinearity.
  2. Why everything sits inside a Pipeline: during cross-validation the imputer, scaler and encoder are re-fitted on each training fold only. If I scaled the whole dataset first, information from the validation fold (its mean and SD) would leak into training and inflate the scores.
  3. make_logreg() – LogisticRegression(solver='saga', max_iter=20_000). saga supports L1, L2 and elastic-net penalties. The function also handles a scikit-learn API change: from 1.8 the penalty is set through l1_ratio, while older versions need penalty='elasticnet'.
  4. The four pipelines: a baseline DummyClassifier(strategy='prior') (always predicts the average rate), LogisticRegression, RandomForestClassifier, HistGradientBoostingClassifier.
  5. Search spaces:
    • logistic regression: C over 11 values from 0.001 to 100 (np.logspace; C = 1 / penalty strength); l1_ratio ∈ {0 = L2, 0.5 = elastic net, 1 = L1}; class_weight ∈ {None, balanced} → 66 combinations;
    • trees: depth, leaf size, number of features, learning rate, L2 penalty and class weights, drawn from distributions (randint, loguniform).
  6. SCORING = {AP, ROC-AUC, Brier} with refit='AP'. Every search records all three metrics but picks the winner on PR-AUC (average precision), the right metric for a 15% target.

Decision: which models compete, and why.

  • Baseline – the floor every model has to beat.
  • Logistic regression – the standard for response models: calibrated probabilities, explainable coefficients, and it works on small data.
  • Random forest – captures non-linear effects and interactions without feature engineering.
  • Gradient boosting – usually the most accurate family on tabular data (scikit-learn's equivalent of XGBoost, which isn't on the allowed list).

Not used:

  • SVM – no native probabilities;
  • k-NN – struggles with mixed feature types and imbalance;
  • Naive Bayes – assumes independent features, but the spend categories are strongly correlated;
  • neural networks – 233 positive examples are far too few.

Output. None – this cell only defines the pipelines and search spaces.

with warnings.catch_warnings():

What I did – step by step

  1. StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42). The training data is split into 5 folds, each with the same 14.7% responders. Each model is trained on 4 folds and scored on the 5th, five times over.
  2. GridSearchCV for logistic regression. All 66 combinations × 5 folds – cheap, so I try everything.
  3. RandomizedSearchCV(n_iter=30) for the trees. With 5–6 hyper-parameters a full grid would be thousands of fits, and random search finds good regions much faster.
  4. n_jobs=-1 uses all CPU cores. warnings.catch_warnings() silences only a harmless scikit-learn UserWarning, so the output stays readable.
  5. Read the best setting and its scores from cv_results_.

Why stratified 5-fold cross-validation – and why I could use it here

  • Cross-validation estimates how a model will do on customers it hasn't seen, using only the training data (the test set stays untouched).
  • It assumes the rows are independent customers from the same population – guaranteed by the de-duplication in Q1b ✓ (a duplicate in both the training and the validation fold would inflate the score).
  • Stratified because only 14.7% respond: every fold gets the same share of responders, so no fold is accidentally "easy".
  • 5 folds, not 10: each validation fold has ~316 customers and ~47 responders – enough to compute PR-AUC reliably. With 10 folds it would be ~23 responders per fold, and the scores would be noisy.

Output and what it means.

  • Logistic regression: PR-AUC 0.702 (ROC-AUC 0.914), with C = 31.6, L1, no class weights.
  • Gradient boosting: 0.644.
  • Random forest: 0.596 – it chose class weights and fully grown trees (min_samples_leaf = 1), a sign of over-fitting.

How to read the numbers

  • PR-AUC (average precision, "AP") – how pure the top of the model's ranking is: the average share of real responders among the customers ranked highest, across all cut-offs. A random model scores the share of responders, 0.147; a perfect one scores 1. 0.70 = about 4.8× better than random.
  • ROC-AUC – the probability that a randomly chosen responder gets a higher score than a randomly chosen non-responder. 0.5 = coin flip, 0.7–0.8 acceptable, 0.8–0.9 excellent, above 0.9 outstanding. 0.914 = outstanding. With an imbalanced target it looks flattering, which is why I select on PR-AUC.
  • C – the inverse of the regularisation strength: small C = strong penalty (simpler model), large C = weak penalty.
In [41]:
# ═══ Q5 — Regularisation curve + 1-SE rule ═══
# How sensitive is logistic regression to the regularisation strength? (validation curve from the grid)
lr_res = pd.DataFrame(searches['Logistic regression'].cv_results_)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
for i, (key, g) in enumerate(lr_res.groupby(['param_clf__l1_ratio', 'param_clf__class_weight'], dropna=False)):
    l1, cw = key
    label = f'{ {0.0: "L2", 0.5: "elastic net", 1.0: "L1"}[float(l1)]}, class_weight={"none" if pd.isna(cw) else cw}'
    g = g.sort_values('param_clf__C')
    ax.plot(g['param_clf__C'].astype(float), g['mean_test_AP'], marker='o', ms=4, lw=1.5, color=PALETTE[i], label=label)
ax.set_xscale('log')
ax.set_xlabel('C (inverse regularisation strength)')
ax.set_ylabel('CV average precision')
ax.axhline(y_train.mean(), color=MUTED, lw=1)
ax.text(1e2, y_train.mean() + 0.015, 'random model', color=MUTED, fontsize=8, ha='right')
ax.legend(fontsize=7.5, ncol=2, loc='lower right')
ax.set_title('Logistic regression: performance plateaus from C = 0.3 upwards')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# One-standard-error rule: the most regularised, unweighted (= calibrated) LR whose CV AP is within 1 SE of the best
best_row = lr_res.loc[lr_res['mean_test_AP'].idxmax()]
threshold_1se = best_row['mean_test_AP'] - best_row['std_test_AP'] / np.sqrt(inner_cv.get_n_splits())
cands = lr_res[(lr_res['mean_test_AP'] >= threshold_1se) & lr_res['param_clf__class_weight'].isna()]
one_se = cands.sort_values(['param_clf__C', 'param_clf__l1_ratio'], ascending=[True, False]).iloc[0]
print(f"Best LR: AP {best_row['mean_test_AP']:.3f} with {best_row['params']}")
print(f"1-SE rule (AP >= {threshold_1se:.3f}): AP {one_se['mean_test_AP']:.3f} with {one_se['params']}")

Best LR: AP 0.702 with {'clf__C': np.float64(31.622776601683793), 'clf__class_weight': None, 'clf__l1_ratio': 1.0}
1-SE rule (AP >= 0.689): AP 0.691 with {'clf__C': np.float64(0.31622776601683794), 'clf__class_weight': None, 'clf__l1_ratio': 0.5}

What I did – step by step

  1. A validation curve: took cv_results_ from the grid search and plotted the mean CV PR-AUC against C (log scale), one line per penalty type and class-weight setting. It shows how sensitive the model is to regularisation.
  2. The one-standard-error rule:
    • the best mean AP is 0.702; its standard error = SD across the 5 folds / √5 = 0.028 / √5 = 0.0125;
    • threshold = best − 1 SE = 0.689;
    • candidates = settings with AP ≥ 0.689 and no class weights;
    • sorted by C ascending (strongest regularisation first), the first row wins.
  3. Why no class weights: class weighting inflates every predicted probability. I need real probabilities, because the business rule is "contact if probability > 27.3%".

Why the 1-SE rule – and why I could use it

  • A CV score is itself an estimate with noise: on other folds the ranking of near-identical settings would shuffle. Everything within one standard error of the best is statistically indistinguishable from it, so I take the simplest (most regularised) of those – it is more likely to hold up on new data. It is the standard rule from Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman.
  • Caveat: the 5 fold scores share training data, so the standard error is approximate – that is why it is a rule of thumb for choosing between equivalent settings, not a formal test.

How to read this chart

  • X axis: C on a log scale (each step = ×10). Left = strong regularisation (coefficients squeezed towards zero, a simpler model); right = weak regularisation (a more flexible model).
  • Y axis: the mean cross-validated PR-AUC over 5 folds – higher = better. The grey horizontal line at 0.147 is a random model.
  • Six lines = 3 penalty types (L2, elastic net, L1) × 2 class-weight settings (balanced or none).
  • What to look for: the point where the curves flatten out (the plateau) – beyond it extra flexibility buys nothing.

What I read from it

  • Left edge (C = 0.001): L1 and elastic net fall to the random line (0.147) – the penalty sets every coefficient to zero, so the model predicts the average for everyone. L2 never sets coefficients exactly to zero, so it keeps 0.56–0.59.
  • From C ≈ 0.3 all six lines lie between 0.68 and 0.70, and from C = 1 between 0.693 and 0.702 → a plateau: performance doesn't depend on the exact setting there.
  • On the plateau the "balanced" lines end slightly lower (0.693–0.694) than the unweighted ones (0.698–0.702).
  • The chosen setting – C = 0.32, elastic net, no class weights: 0.691 – sits at the left edge of the plateau, within one standard error of the best (0.702 at C = 31.6).

Output and what it means. The 1-SE rule picks C = 0.32 with an elastic net (l1_ratio = 0.5), with CV AP 0.691 vs 0.702 – about 100× stronger regularisation than the best setting (C = 31.6), at a cost smaller than the noise of the estimate.

How to read the numbers

  • AP 0.702 / 0.691 – mean CV PR-AUC (random = 0.147, perfect = 1).
  • Standard error 0.0125 – how much the mean CV score itself could move with other folds. A difference of 0.011 (0.702 − 0.691) is smaller than that → not a real difference.
  • l1_ratio – 0 = L2 (shrinks all coefficients), 1 = L1 (sets weak ones exactly to zero), 0.5 = elastic net (both).

# ═══ Q5 — Option 2: nested cross-validation ═══
# Option 2 - NESTED cross-validation: an unbiased estimate of each *tuning procedure* (outer 5 folds x inner 3 folds).
# The inner-CV scores above are optimistic because the same folds chose the hyperparameters.
outer_cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=7)
nested_inner = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
nested = {}
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter('ignore', category=UserWarning)
    nested['Baseline (always predict the base rate)'] = cross_validate(pipes['Baseline (always predict the base rate)'],
                                                                       X_train, y_train, cv=outer_cv, scoring=SCORING)
    for name in ['Logistic regression', 'Random forest', 'Gradient boosting']:
        nested[name] = cross_validate(make_search(name, nested_inner, n_iter=20), X_train, y_train, cv=outer_cv,
                                      scoring=SCORING, n_jobs=1)

nested_tbl = pd.DataFrame({name: {'AP mean': r['test_AP'].mean(), 'AP sd': r['test_AP'].std(),
                                  'ROC-AUC mean': r['test_ROC_AUC'].mean(), 'ROC-AUC sd': r['test_ROC_AUC'].std(),
                                  'Brier mean': -r['test_Brier'].mean()} for name, r in nested.items()}).T
# paired comparison on the SAME outer folds
d_lr_gb = nested['Logistic regression']['test_AP'] - nested['Gradient boosting']['test_AP']
d_lr_rf = nested['Logistic regression']['test_AP'] - nested['Random forest']['test_AP']
print(f'Paired AP difference, LR - GB: {d_lr_gb.mean():+.3f} (fold-level sd {d_lr_gb.std():.3f}); '
      f'LR - RF: {d_lr_rf.mean():+.3f} (sd {d_lr_rf.std():.3f}); LR wins on {np.sum(d_lr_gb > 0)}/5 and {np.sum(d_lr_rf > 0)}/5 folds')
nested_tbl.round(3)

What I did – step by step

  1. The problem: the scores from the tuning step are optimistic, because the same folds were used both to choose the hyper-parameters and to measure them.

  2. Nested cross-validation: cross_validate(make_search(name, nested_inner, n_iter=20), X_train, y_train, cv=outer_cv).

    • The outer loop (5 folds) holds out one fold;
    • the inner loop (3 folds) runs the whole tuning procedure on the remaining data;
    • the tuned model is then scored on the held-out outer fold, which it has never seen.

    The result is an unbiased estimate of the whole procedure.

  3. Paired comparison: all models use the same outer folds, so I compare them fold by fold and count the wins.

Why nested CV and a paired comparison – and why I could use them

  • Nested CV is the standard way to measure "tuning + model" honestly. It needs the same thing as ordinary CV – independent customers ✓ – plus enough data for an inner split: each inner training set still has ~840 customers and ~125 responders ✓.
  • Paired by fold: some folds are simply easier than others. Comparing models on the same fold removes that noise, just like a paired test compares the same customers before and after. With only 5 folds I report the wins and the mean difference instead of a formal paired t-test – 5 points are too few for a reliable p-value, while "5 of 5" is easy to read.

Output and what it means.

  • Logistic regression 0.71 ± 0.04, gradient boosting 0.64, random forest 0.60, baseline 0.15.
  • Logistic regression wins on 5 of 5 folds against both (+0.07 AP vs gradient boosting, +0.11 vs the forest).

Why the simple model wins: the data is small (233 positive examples), and the signal is mostly monotonic – more previous acceptances and more recent purchases mean more response. A linear model captures that with few parameters; the trees spend their flexibility on noise.

How to read the numbers

  • 0.71 ± 0.04 – mean PR-AUC over the 5 outer folds ± its standard deviation (how much it varies from fold to fold). The baseline 0.15 is the "random" level.
  • Wins 5 of 5 – in every one of the five held-out folds logistic regression scored higher. If the two models were equally good, that would happen by chance only 1 time in 32.

Test-set evaluation (Q5a/b)¶

In [43]:
# ═══ Q5a/b — Test-set evaluation (all models) ═══
# Final evaluation on the untouched TEST set (all tuned models reported; the 1-SE logistic regression was chosen BEFORE this step)
def bootstrap_metric(y_true, score, metric, n_boot=2000, seed=RANDOM_STATE):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    y_true, score = np.asarray(y_true), np.asarray(score)
    vals = []
    for _ in range(n_boot):
        idx = rng.integers(0, len(y_true), len(y_true))
        if y_true[idx].min() == y_true[idx].max():
            continue
        vals.append(metric(y_true[idx], score[idx]))
    return np.percentile(vals, [2.5, 97.5])

lr_1se = sklearn.base.clone(pipes['Logistic regression']).set_params(**one_se['params']).fit(X_train, y_train)
fitted = {'Logistic regression (1-SE, final)': lr_1se,
          'Logistic regression (best CV AP)': searches['Logistic regression'].best_estimator_,
          'Random forest': searches['Random forest'].best_estimator_,
          'Gradient boosting': searches['Gradient boosting'].best_estimator_}
test_scores = {name: m.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] for name, m in fitted.items()}
rows = []
for name, p in test_scores.items():
    ap_ci = bootstrap_metric(y_test, p, average_precision_score)
    auc_ci = bootstrap_metric(y_test, p, roc_auc_score)
    top10 = np.argsort(-p)[:int(np.ceil(0.1 * len(p)))]
    rows.append({'model': name, 'ROC-AUC': roc_auc_score(y_test, p), 'ROC-AUC 95% CI': tuple(auc_ci.round(3)),
                 'PR-AUC (AP)': average_precision_score(y_test, p), 'AP 95% CI': tuple(ap_ci.round(3)),
                 'Brier': brier_score_loss(y_test, p), 'log loss': log_loss(y_test, p),
                 'lift @ top 10%': y_test.iloc[top10].mean() / y_test.mean()})
rows.append({'model': 'Baseline', 'ROC-AUC': 0.5, 'PR-AUC (AP)': y_test.mean(),
             'Brier': brier_score_loss(y_test, np.full(len(y_test), y_train.mean())), 'lift @ top 10%': 1.0})
test_tbl = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('model')
test_tbl.round(3)

Random forest 0.874 (0.834, 0.911) 0.508 (0.392, 0.642) 0.094 0.291 3.575
Gradient boosting 0.886 (0.847, 0.921) 0.592 (0.475, 0.709) 0.088 0.276 4.427
Baseline 0.500 NaN 0.147 NaN 0.125 NaN 1.000

What I did – step by step

  1. The final 1-SE model: sklearn.base.clone(pipes['Logistic regression']).set_params(**one_se['params']).fit(X_train, y_train) – a fresh copy with the chosen settings, trained on the full training set.
  2. Test probabilities from every tuned model: predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1].
  3. Metrics:
    • roc_auc_score – overall ranking quality;
    • average_precision_score (PR-AUC) – ranking quality among the top-ranked customers we would actually contact;
    • brier_score_loss – the mean squared error of the probabilities, i.e. calibration;
    • log_loss;
    • lift at the top 10% – the response rate among the 10% highest scores ÷ the overall rate.
  4. bootstrap_metric() – 2,000 resamples of the 395 test customers, recomputing AUC and AP each time and taking the 2.5–97.5 percentiles.

Why bootstrap confidence intervals – and why I could use them here

  • With only 58 responders in the test set, a single number hides a lot of uncertainty. AUC and AP have no simple formula for their confidence interval, so I resample.
  • The bootstrap needs independent test customers ✓ (one row per customer) and a test set that represents the population ✓ (stratified split, 14.7% responders).

Output and what it means. The final model reaches:

  • ROC-AUC 0.906 (95% CI 0.87–0.94);
  • PR-AUC 0.662 (95% CI 0.55–0.76) vs 0.147 for random;
  • Brier 0.080 vs 0.125 for the baseline;
  • lift 4.4× – the top 10% respond at ~65% vs 14.7% on average.

Gradient boosting scores 0.59 and the forest 0.51. The test results agree with nested CV, so the model is not over-fitted.

How to read the numbers

  • ROC-AUC 0.906 – a random responder outranks a random non-responder 91% of the time (0.5 = coin flip, above 0.9 = outstanding).
  • PR-AUC 0.662 – read against the random level 0.147: about 4.5× better than random.
  • Brier score – the average of (predicted probability − actual 0/1)²: 0 = perfect, lower = better. Always predicting the base rate scores 0.147 × 0.853 = 0.125; the model scores 0.080 – 36% better.
  • Log loss – like Brier, but punishes confident wrong predictions harder; lower = better.
  • Lift 4.4× – the top 10% of scores respond 4.4 times more often than the average customer.
  • 95% CI – the range the metric would plausibly take on another sample of 395 customers. AP 0.55–0.76 is wide (only 58 responders), but even its lower end is 3.7× random.
In [44]:
# ═══ Q5b — Why not accuracy, thresholds, calibration ═══
# Why accuracy is the wrong metric: a model that never contacts anyone is "85% accurate"
final_name = 'Logistic regression (1-SE, final)'
final_model = fitted[final_name]
p_test = test_scores[final_name]
acc_all_zero = (y_test == 0).mean()
acc_model = ((p_test >= 0.5).astype(int) == y_test).mean()
print(f'Accuracy of "nobody responds": {acc_all_zero:.1%}  vs  model at 0.5 threshold: {acc_model:.1%} '
      f'-> a {100 * (acc_model - acc_all_zero):.1f} pp difference hides a model that actually finds responders.')

# Out-of-fold predictions on TRAIN (final hyperparameters) are used to choose thresholds - never the test set
oof = cross_val_predict(final_model, X_train, y_train, cv=inner_cv, method='predict_proba')[:, 1]

def profit(y_true, contact):
    y_true, contact = np.asarray(y_true).astype(bool), np.asarray(contact).astype(bool)
    return REVENUE_PER_RESPONSE * (y_true & contact).sum() - COST_PER_CONTACT * contact.sum()

grid = np.linspace(0.02, 0.9, 89)
oof_profit = np.array([profit(y_train, oof >= t) for t in grid])
oof_f1 = np.array([f1_score(y_train, oof >= t) for t in grid])
t_profit, t_f1 = grid[oof_profit.argmax()], grid[oof_f1.argmax()]
print(f'Thresholds chosen on out-of-fold TRAIN predictions: profit-optimal = {t_profit:.2f}, F1-optimal = {t_f1:.2f}, '
      f'theoretical break-even for calibrated probabilities = {BREAK_EVEN_RATE:.3f}')

# Calibration: is a predicted 30% really 30%?
frac_pos, mean_pred = calibration_curve(y_train, oof, n_bins=8, strategy='quantile')
print('Calibration (OOF, quantile bins) - mean predicted vs observed rate:',
      [f'{m:.2f}->{f:.2f}' for m, f in zip(mean_pred, frac_pos)])

Accuracy of "nobody responds": 85.3%  vs  model at 0.5 threshold: 88.9% -> a 3.5 pp difference hides a model that actually finds responders.

Thresholds chosen on out-of-fold TRAIN predictions: profit-optimal = 0.26, F1-optimal = 0.26, theoretical break-even for calibrated probabilities = 0.273
Calibration (OOF, quantile bins) - mean predicted vs observed rate: ['0.00->0.00', '0.01->0.01', '0.02->0.01', '0.03->0.02', '0.06->0.05', '0.12->0.15', '0.26->0.29', '0.68->0.66']

What I did – step by step

  1. Accuracy check: (y_test == 0).mean() is the accuracy of always predicting "nobody responds". I compared it with the model at a 0.5 threshold.
  2. Out-of-fold probabilities on the training data: cross_val_predict(final_model, X_train, y_train, cv=inner_cv, method='predict_proba'). Every training customer gets a score from a model that didn't see them. Why: thresholds are chosen on these scores, so the test set stays untouched.
  3. profit(y, contact) = 11 × responders reached − 3 × customers contacted, evaluated for 89 thresholds from 0.02 to 0.90 (np.linspace). The best threshold is grid[profit.argmax()]. The F1-optimal threshold is found the same way, for comparison.
  4. calibration_curve(y_train, oof, n_bins=8, strategy='quantile') – customers sorted into 8 equal-sized groups by predicted probability, comparing average predicted vs actually observed response.

Why these checks – and why I could use them

  • Out-of-fold predictions are needed because a model scores its own training customers too optimistically. They require the same as CV – independent customers ✓.
  • Quantile bins (8 groups of ~198 customers) make every point on the calibration curve rest on the same number of customers, so each observed rate is equally precise. Equal-width bins would leave the high-probability bins with only a handful of customers.

Output and what it means.

  • "Nobody responds" is 85.3% accurate; the model is 88.9%. That 3.5-point difference hides a model that actually finds responders – and accuracy treats a wasted contact (−3) the same as a missed responder (−8). That is why I use PR-AUC, calibration and profit instead.
  • The profit-optimal threshold on the training data is 0.26 – practically the theoretical break-even 0.273 (= 3/11).
  • Calibration: predicted 0.26 → observed 0.29; predicted 0.68 → observed 0.66.

The model's probabilities can be read literally, so the 27.3% rule is valid.

How to read the numbers

  • Accuracy – the share of correct yes/no predictions. With 85% non-responders, "predict nobody" already scores 85%, so accuracy says almost nothing here.
  • Threshold – the predicted probability above which a customer is contacted. Break-even 3/11 = 0.273: at that probability the expected revenue (11 × 0.273) equals the cost of the contact (3).
  • Calibration pairs "predicted → observed" – a well-calibrated model has the two numbers close: among customers the model gives ~26%, 29% actually responded. If the model said 26% and only 10% responded, the 27.3% rule would be meaningless.
  • F1-optimal threshold – the threshold that balances precision and recall; shown only to make the point that it ignores the costs, unlike the profit threshold.

What I did – step by step

  1. Each targeting rule as a True/False "contact" vector on the test set:
    • everyone;
    • the rule of thumb (X_test[CMP_COLS].sum(axis=1) > 0);
    • model thresholds 0.5, 0.26 and 0.273;
    • a fixed budget (the top 20% by np.argsort(-p));
    • perfect foresight, as the ceiling.
  2. confusion_matrix(y_test, contact).ravel() → responders reached (TP), wasted contacts (FP) and missed responders (FN); then precision, recall, profit() and profit per 1,000 customers.

Output.

Rule Contacted Responders reached Profit per 1,000 customers

How to read the table

  • Contacted – the share of customers the rule would send the offer to (= cost).
  • Responders reached (recall) – of all customers who would accept, the share the rule reaches.
  • Precision (in the full output) – of the contacted customers, the share who accept; above 27.3% each contact pays for itself on average.
  • TP / FP / FN – responders reached / wasted contacts / missed responders.
  • Profit per 1,000 customers – 11 × responders reached − 3 × contacts, scaled to 1,000 customers so the rules can be compared directly.

Decision: contact customers above the break-even threshold of 27.3%.

  • It comes from the economics – contact when 11 × probability > 3 – so nothing is fitted to the data, and it can't over-fit.
  • It is valid because the model is calibrated, and the data-driven optimum (0.26) confirms it.
  • It earned the most of all the rules that can be fixed in advance.

Other rules have their place: a fixed budget when spend is set before the campaign, a lower threshold for reach campaigns, a higher one when contact fatigue matters. If the economics change, so does the threshold – with a 40% margin it would be 3 / 4.4 ≈ 68%.

Top 20% of test customers by score contain 66% of all responders; best achievable profit on the curve = 243 MU when contacting the top 24% (perfect foresight = 464 MU)

What I did. Four charts:

  1. Cumulative gains – customers sorted by score (np.argsort(-p_test)), and the cumsum() of responders ÷ all responders as we go down the list.
  2. Profit vs depth of targeting – cumulative profit (11 × responders − 3 × contacts) when contacting the top k customers.
  3. Calibration – the out-of-fold reliability curve from the previous cell.
  4. Profit vs threshold on the training data (out-of-fold), with lines at the data-driven optimum and the break-even.

(Charts 1–2 use the 395 test customers; charts 3–4 the 1,580 training customers' out-of-fold scores, so the threshold is never chosen on the test set.)

How to read this chart – panel by panel

  1. Cumulative gains. X = share of customers contacted, starting with the highest score; Y = share of all responders reached. The grey diagonal = picking customers at random (10% contacted → 10% of responders). The higher the blue curve above the diagonal, the better the model ranks.
  2. Profit vs depth. X = share contacted (highest score first); Y = campaign profit in MU on the test customers. The grey line is 0. The curve rises while the next customers are mostly responders and falls once most of them are wasted contacts.
  3. Calibration. X = predicted probability (the average of a group of ~198 customers); Y = the share of that group that actually responded. Points on the diagonal = the probabilities are honest. Above the diagonal = the model underestimates; below = it overestimates.
  4. Profit vs threshold. X = the probability threshold (contact everyone above it); Y = profit on the training customers. Blue vertical line = the threshold with the highest profit (0.26); red = the theoretical break-even (0.273).

What I read from it

  1. Gains: contacting the top 10% reaches 43% of responders, the top 20% → 66%, the top 30% → 90%, the top half → 95%. Random selection would give 10 / 20 / 30 / 50%. Almost all responders sit in the top third of the scores.
  2. Profit: rises to a peak of +243 at 24% contacted, then falls; it drops below zero once more than ~51% of customers are contacted, and contacting everyone ends at −547.
  3. Calibration: the 8 points lie close to the diagonal – e.g. predicted 0.06 → observed 0.05, 0.12 → 0.15, 0.26 → 0.29, 0.68 → 0.66. Slight under-estimation in the middle and slight over-estimation at the top, both small. The low points (predicted below 3%) all have almost no responders, as they should.
  4. Threshold: profit climbs steeply from −668 (threshold 0.02 = contact almost everyone) to a broad, flat top of ~900 between ~0.2 and ~0.3, peaking at 934 at 0.26; at the break-even 0.273 it is 917 – only 17 less. At 0.5 it falls to 789, and at 0.9 to 217 (too few contacted). A flat top means the exact threshold within 0.2–0.3 hardly matters – the economic 27.3% is safe.

Output and what it means. The model concentrates the responders at the top of the list; profit peaks at roughly the top quarter of customers; the probabilities are honest; and the profit-optimal threshold coincides with the break-even. Perfect foresight would earn +464 on the test set, so the 27.3% rule (+191) captures about 40% of the theoretical ceiling.

How to read the numbers

  • "Top 20% → 66% of responders" – the model's lift at 20%: 66 / 20 = 3.3× better than random at that depth.
  • Profit in MU – 11 per responder reached − 3 per contact, on the 395 test customers (×2.5 ≈ per 1,000).
  • Calibration pairs – "predicted → observed"; the closer, the more the probabilities can be taken literally.

The final model — why this one¶

In [47]:
# ═══ Q5 — Decision 6: all models on equal terms ═══
# Every candidate on equal terms: each model gets its OWN profit-optimal threshold, chosen on its out-of-fold TRAIN
# predictions (a model with inflated probabilities is not penalised for not matching the 27.3% rule)
nested_name = {'Logistic regression (1-SE, final)': 'Logistic regression', 'Logistic regression (best CV AP)': 'Logistic regression',
               'Random forest': 'Random forest', 'Gradient boosting': 'Gradient boosting'}
rows, oof_store = [], {}
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter('ignore', category=UserWarning)
    for name, m in fitted.items():
        oof_m = cross_val_predict(m, X_train, y_train, cv=inner_cv, method='predict_proba')[:, 1]
        t_m = grid[np.argmax([profit(y_train, oof_m >= t) for t in grid])]
        oof_store[name] = (oof_m, t_m)
        p = test_scores[name]
        rows.append({'model': name, 'nested CV AP (tuning procedure)': nested[nested_name[name]]['test_AP'].mean(),
                     'test AP': average_precision_score(y_test, p), 'test ROC-AUC': roc_auc_score(y_test, p),
                     'test Brier': brier_score_loss(y_test, p), 'own threshold (OOF)': t_m,
                     'test profit @ own threshold': profit(y_test, p >= t_m),
                     'test profit @ 27.3%': profit(y_test, p >= BREAK_EVEN_RATE)})
comparison = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('model')
comparison['profit / 1,000 customers @ own threshold'] = 1000 * comparison['test profit @ own threshold'] / len(y_test)
comparison.round(3)

What I did. A fair comparison of all four models. For each one, cross_val_predict gives out-of-fold probabilities on the training data, and from those I pick its own profit-optimal threshold (grid[np.argmax(profit)]). Then I compute test PR-AUC, ROC-AUC, Brier, and test profit both at its own threshold and at 27.3%. Why own thresholds: a model with inflated probabilities (the forest, with class weights) shouldn't be penalised just because 27.3% doesn't suit it.

Output and what it means. Logistic regression wins on every column:

  • Nested PR-AUC: 0.71, vs 0.64 for gradient boosting and 0.60 for the forest.
  • Test PR-AUC: 0.66, vs 0.59 and 0.51.
  • Brier: 0.080, vs 0.088 and 0.094.
  • Profit: +182 / +191 for the 1-SE model, vs +154 (gradient boosting) and +151 (forest), even at their own optimised thresholds.

The lightly regularised logistic regression earned +216 at its own threshold (0.15) – examined in the next cell.

How to read the numbers

  • Nested PR-AUC – the honest estimate from nested CV (higher = better; random 0.147).
  • Test PR-AUC / ROC-AUC – the same metrics on the untouched test set.
  • Brier – the error of the probabilities (lower = better; 0.125 = always predicting the average).
  • Profit (own threshold / 27.3%) – MU earned on the 395 test customers, at the threshold each model chose for itself on its training data, and at the economic break-even.
In [48]:
# ═══ Q5 — Decision 6: profit uncertainty (paired bootstrap) ═══
# How certain are these profit differences?
# (a) the business comparison that can be made BEFORE the test set: out-of-fold profit on the training data
# (b) paired bootstrap of the TEST profit difference vs. the final model at the break-even threshold
yt = y_test.to_numpy()
boot_idx = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE).integers(0, len(yt), (5000, len(yt)))

def boot_profit(contact):
    c, yy = contact[boot_idx], yt[boot_idx]
    return REVENUE_PER_RESPONSE * (c & (yy == 1)).sum(axis=1) - COST_PER_CONTACT * c.sum(axis=1)

ref_contact = test_scores[final_name] >= BREAK_EVEN_RATE
ref_boot = boot_profit(ref_contact)
rows = [{'model / rule': f'{final_name} @ 27.3%',
         'OOF profit on train (pre-test)': profit(y_train, oof_store[final_name][0] >= BREAK_EVEN_RATE),
         'test profit': profit(y_test, ref_contact), 'difference vs final': 0, '95% CI of difference': '-',
         'P(better than final)': '-'}]
for name in fitted:
    oof_m, t_m = oof_store[name]
    contact = test_scores[name] >= t_m
    diff = boot_profit(contact) - ref_boot
    lo, hi = np.percentile(diff, [2.5, 97.5])
    rows.append({'model / rule': f'{name} @ own threshold {t_m:.2f}', 'OOF profit on train (pre-test)': profit(y_train, oof_m >= t_m),
                 'test profit': profit(y_test, contact), 'difference vs final': profit(y_test, contact) - profit(y_test, ref_contact),
                 '95% CI of difference': f'{lo:+.0f} to {hi:+.0f}', 'P(better than final)': f'{(diff > 0).mean():.0%}'})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('model / rule')

What I did.

  1. A paired bootstrap on the test set: 5,000 resampled test sets (np.random.default_rng(42).integers(0, 395, (5000, 395))). boot_profit() computes the profit of each model on the same resampled customers, and the 2.5–97.5 percentiles of the difference vs the final model give a 95% CI.
  2. Out-of-fold profit on the training data – the comparison that can be made before touching the test set.

Why a paired bootstrap – and why I could use it here

  • Profit is a sum over a few dozen responders, so it jumps around from sample to sample, and there is no textbook formula for the uncertainty of a difference in profit.
  • Paired: both models are judged on identical resampled customers, so the "luck of the sample" cancels out and only the difference between the models remains. An unpaired comparison would be far noisier.
  • Needs only independent test customers ✓.

Output and what it means.

  • The best-CV logistic regression at threshold 0.15 earned +25 more on the test set (216 vs 191) and more out-of-fold (977 vs 917).
  • But the 95% CI of the difference is −30 to +87: it includes zero, and in 20% of resamples it does worse. Not significant.
  • Gradient boosting and the forest are about 37–40 lower (also not significant individually, but consistently behind).

How to read the numbers

  • 95% CI of the profit difference – the plausible range of how much more (or less) the alternative would earn. If it contains 0, the data can't tell the two models apart.
  • "Worse in 20% of resamples" – a bootstrap version of "how sure are we": the alternative is better in 80% of plausible test sets – not convincing (you'd want 95%+).

# ═══ Q5 — Decision 6: stability of the final 1-SE model ═══
# What characterises the 1-SE model vs. the best-CV model? Size, sparsity and STABILITY of the coefficients:
# refit both on 50 bootstrap resamples of the training data and see how much the coefficients move.
def coef_vector(model):
    return pd.Series(model.named_steps['clf'].coef_.ravel(), index=model.named_steps['prep'].get_feature_names_out())

lr_variants = {'1-SE (C = 0.32, elastic net)': lr_1se, 'best CV (C = 31.6, L1)': searches['Logistic regression'].best_estimator_}
rng = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE)
boot_coefs = {k: [] for k in lr_variants}
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter('ignore')
    for b in range(50):
        idx = rng.integers(0, len(X_train), len(X_train))
        for k, m in lr_variants.items():
            boot_coefs[k].append(coef_vector(sklearn.base.clone(m).fit(X_train.iloc[idx], y_train.iloc[idx])))
rows = []
for k, m in lr_variants.items():
    c, Bc = coef_vector(m), pd.DataFrame(boot_coefs[k])
    nz = c != 0
    rows.append({'model': k, 'non-zero coefficients': f'{int(nz.sum())} of {len(c)}',
                 'largest |coefficient|': c.abs().max(), 'sum of |coefficients|': c.abs().sum(),
                 'mean bootstrap SD of a coefficient': Bc.std().mean(),
                 'sign flips / drops to zero across bootstraps': (np.sign(Bc.loc[:, nz]) != np.sign(c[nz])).to_numpy().mean(),
                 'test AP': average_precision_score(y_test, m.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]),
                 'test Brier': brier_score_loss(y_test, m.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('model').round(3)
