What I did. The stability of the two logistic-regression variants: both refitted on 50 bootstrap samples of the training data (sklearn.base.clone(m).fit(X_train.iloc[idx], y_train.iloc[idx])). For each I measure:

  • how big the coefficients are – the largest and the sum;
  • how much each coefficient moves across refits – the mean SD;
  • how often a coefficient flips sign or drops to zero.

Why a bootstrap refit – and why I could use it

  • It simulates "what if we had collected a slightly different set of customers?" – exactly the question for a model that will be used on the next campaign. It needs independent customers ✓.

Output and what it means.

  • Same accuracy: test PR-AUC 0.662 vs 0.666, Brier 0.080 vs 0.081.
  • Smaller coefficients: largest 1.15 vs 1.79, sum 13.5 vs 21.4.
  • About 40% less variable across refits: mean SD 0.155 vs 0.271.
  • Sign flips are equally rare in both (~7%), so both tell the same story – the 1-SE model just tells it with steadier numbers.

How to read the numbers

  • Mean SD of the coefficients – how much a coefficient changes when the model is refitted on a different sample: lower = steadier. 0.155 vs 0.271 → the 1-SE model's coefficients move about 40% less.
  • Sign flips – how often a feature switches between "raises" and "lowers" the response across refits; a high rate would mean the direction can't be trusted.

Decision: the final model is the logistic regression with an elastic-net penalty, selected with the 1-SE rule, without class weights.

  1. Best model family on every view (nested CV, test, profit).
  2. Equal accuracy, steadier coefficients – a safer bet for the next campaign.
  3. It needs the regularisation: only 7 events per parameter, and strongly correlated spend features (VIF up to 24, see Appendix).
  4. Calibrated probabilities, which the 27.3% rule depends on.
  5. Explainable: every coefficient is an odds ratio.

What I gave up: a possible +25 profit on the test set (not significant) from the lighter version with a data-driven threshold. I chose stability and a transparent rule over a gain that may be noise.

Top drivers (Q5c)¶

# Lens 2 & 3: GROUPED permutation importance on the TEST set (model-agnostic). Correlated columns (e.g. the 5 campaign
# flags, the 7 spend columns) are shuffled together, otherwise each one looks unimportant because the others cover for it.
FEATURE_GROUPS = {
    'Campaign history (Cmp1-5)': CMP_COLS, 'Recency': ['Recency'], 'Tenure': ['TenureYears'],
    'Spend by category + order value': LOG_FEATURES,
    'Purchase channels & deals': ['NumDealsPurchases', 'NumWebPurchases', 'NumCatalogPurchases', 'NumStorePurchases'],
    'Web visits': ['NumWebVisitsMonth'], 'Kids & teens at home': ['Kidhome', 'Teenhome'], 'Marital status': ['Marital_Status'],
    'Education': ['Education'], 'Income': ['Income'], 'Age': ['Age'], 'Complain': ['Complain'],
}

def grouped_permutation_importance(model, X_, y_, groups, n_repeats=50, seed=RANDOM_STATE):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    base = average_precision_score(y_, model.predict_proba(X_)[:, 1])
    out = {}
    for gname, cols in groups.items():
        drops = []
        for _ in range(n_repeats):
            Xp = X_.copy()
            Xp[cols] = X_[cols].to_numpy()[rng.permutation(len(X_))]
            drops.append(base - average_precision_score(y_, model.predict_proba(Xp)[:, 1]))
        out[gname] = (np.mean(drops), np.std(drops))
    return pd.DataFrame(out, index=['mean', 'sd']).T

perm = {name: grouped_permutation_importance(fitted[name], X_test, y_test, FEATURE_GROUPS)
        for name in [final_name, 'Gradient boosting']}
perm_tbl = pd.concat(perm, axis=1)
perm_top = perm_tbl.sort_values((final_name, 'mean'), ascending=True)
yy = np.arange(len(perm_top))
for i, name in enumerate(perm):
    axes[1].barh(yy + (i - 0.5) * 0.38, perm_top[(name, 'mean')], xerr=perm_top[(name, 'sd')], height=0.36,
                 color=PALETTE[i], label=name.replace(' (1-SE, final)', ''), error_kw=dict(ecolor=MUTED, lw=1))
axes[1].set_yticks(yy)
axes[1].set_yticklabels(perm_top.index)
axes[1].set_title('Grouped permutation importance (test): drop in AP when shuffled')
axes[1].legend(loc='lower right')
axes[1].grid(axis='y', visible=False)
plt.tight_layout()

print('Rank agreement of grouped importances, LR vs GB (Spearman):',

What I did – step by step

  1. Coefficients: final_model.named_steps['clf'].coef_ paired with named_steps['prep'].get_feature_names_out() – the feature names after preprocessing. Every feature is standardised, so each coefficient is the effect of +1 standard deviation, and np.exp(coef) turns it into an odds ratio. I plotted the top 15.
  2. grouped_permutation_importance() – my own version of permutation importance: a group of columns (e.g. all 5 campaign flags, or all 7 spend columns) is shuffled together 50 times, and I measure the drop in test PR-AUC.
  3. Ran it for two different model families – the final logistic regression and gradient boosting – and measured agreement with stats.spearmanr on their importance rankings.

Why these two methods – and why I could use them here

  • Standardised coefficients are comparable with each other because every input is on the same scale (mean 0, SD 1) ✓. Two caveats: the penalty shrinks them towards zero (so read their order and direction, not their exact size), and correlated inputs share the credit between them.
  • Permutation importance works for any model (so the linear model and the trees can be compared on one scale) and is measured on the test set, which neither model saw ✓. It assumes that shuffling a column destroys its information without creating impossible customers – which fails for correlated columns (shuffling one, the others still carry the information). That is why I shuffle correlated columns together as a group. 50 repeats give a mean and a standard deviation.
  • Spearman rank correlation between the two importance lists compares rankings, which is what "do the models agree on what matters" means.

How to read this chart

  • Left – coefficients. One bar per input (the 15 strongest). Blue, to the right of 0 = raises the chance of accepting; orange, to the left = lowers it. Longer bar = stronger. The label OR = odds ratio = e^coefficient:
    • for a number (e.g. Recency): the change in the odds of accepting for +1 standard deviation of that input, everything else equal;
    • for a category (e.g. Marital_Status_Single): the odds compared with the reference group – Graduation for education, Married for marital status.
    • OR 1 = no effect; 3.17 = odds ×3.2; 0.39 = odds ×0.39 (−61%).
  • Right – grouped permutation importance. One pair of bars per group of inputs: how much the model's test PR-AUC drops when that group is randomly shuffled. Blue = logistic regression, orange = gradient boosting. The longer the bar, the more the model relies on that information. The thin grey line through each bar = ± 1 standard deviation over the 50 shuffles. A bar whose grey line crosses 0 = the model doesn't really use that information.

What I read from it

  • Right panel: campaign history is by far the most important for both models (AP drop 0.28 for LR, 0.21 for GB), then Recency (0.09 / 0.09), purchase channels & deals (0.09 / 0.06), tenure (0.06 / 0.07), kids & teens (0.05 / 0.03), spend (0.05 / 0.04) and marital status (0.03 / 0.04). Education and web visits are small; income, age and complaints ≈ 0 – their bars sit inside ± 1 SD of zero.
  • Both models rank the groups almost identically (Spearman 0.96) → the drivers are a property of the data, not of one algorithm.
  • Left panel: Single customers ×3.17 vs married (Divorced ×2.08, Widow ×2.14); PhD ×2.85 and Master ×1.67 vs Graduation; +1 SD of meat spend ×2.94; +1 SD of days since the last purchase ×0.39; +1 SD of tenure ×2.26; +1 SD of wine spend ×0.46; store purchases ×0.52; teenagers ×0.62; catalogue purchases ×1.43; web visits ×1.39; earlier campaigns 3 and 5 ×1.67 and ×1.56.
  • Why campaign history tops the right panel but its single flags are only mid-table on the left: the 5 campaign flags share the credit – each alone has an OR of ~1.5–1.7, but shuffling all five at once removes the strongest signal in the data.
  • Why income and age are ≈ 0 on the right although they mattered in Q3/Q4: their information is already carried by spend, family and channel variables, so removing them costs the model nothing.

Output and what it means.

  • The two models agree almost perfectly (Spearman 0.96).
  • Young kids → 0 (removed by the L1 part of the penalty – consistent with Q4, where young kids didn't affect response).
  • Reading note: wine (−) and meat (+) have opposite signs only because spend categories are correlated – together they describe the basket mix at a given total. That is why the driver story relies on grouped importance and observed rates, not on single coefficients.

How to read the numbers

  • Odds ratio per SD – 1 = no effect; above 1 raises, below 1 lowers the odds of accepting. Odds are p / (1 − p): at a 15% base rate, odds ×2 is roughly 15% → 26%.
  • Drop in AP – how much worse the ranking gets without that information (test AP of the final model = 0.66). 0.28 = without campaign history the model loses over 40% of its AP.
  • Spearman 0.96 – rank agreement from −1 to 1; 0.96 = practically the same ranking.

What I did. Translated the drivers into business numbers: pd.cut(Recency, [...]), pd.qcut(TenureYears, 4) and pd.cut(NumCatalogPurchases, [...]) create bands, then groupby(...)['Response'].mean() gives the observed response rate per band – no model involved. Why no model: observed rates need no assumptions and are what Marketing can check in its own reports.

Output – the top 3 drivers, with observed response rates:

  1. Campaign history: 8% with no earlier acceptance, 30% with one, 52% with two, 82% with three or more.
  2. Recency: 29% for customers who bought in the last 20 days vs 6% after 80–100 days.
  3. Channel: heavy catalogue buyers (6+ purchases) respond at 31%, vs 4% for customers who never buy by catalogue.

Also: the longest-tenured quarter responds at 26% vs 9% for the newest; households with teenagers 8% vs 21% without; couples 11% vs 22% for singles.

How to read the numbers – each rate is simply "of the customers in this band, the share who accepted the last campaign". Compare it with the 27.3% break-even: bands above it are worth contacting as a whole, bands below it only through the model's individual scores.

Recommendation. Contact customers who said yes before, bought recently and shop by catalogue – and let the model's score decide who is above 27%.

# ═══ Q5c — Decision 7: feature-set variants (robustness) ═══
# Robustness: how much do we lose without (a) Recency (possible timing leakage), (b) demographic attributes
# (fairness-through-unawareness), (c) campaign history (cold-start customers)? Same LR settings, repeated CV on train.
best_lr = one_se['params']
variants = {
    'All features (final model)': FEATURES,
    'Without Recency': [f for f in FEATURES if f != 'Recency'],
    'Without demographics (Age, Kids, Marital, Education)': [f for f in FEATURES if f not in
                                                             ['Age', 'Kidhome', 'Teenhome', 'Marital_Status', 'Education']],
    'Without Recency AND demographics': [f for f in FEATURES if f not in
                                         ['Recency', 'Age', 'Kidhome', 'Teenhome', 'Marital_Status', 'Education']],
    'Without previous-campaign history': [f for f in FEATURES if f not in CMP_COLS],
}
rcv = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=3, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
rows = []
for name, cols in variants.items():
    pipe = Pipeline([('prep', make_preprocessor([c for c in LOG_FEATURES if c in cols], [c for c in NUM_FEATURES if c in cols],
                                                [c for c in CAT_FEATURES if c in cols])), ('clf', make_logreg())])
    pipe.set_params(**best_lr)
    r = cross_validate(pipe, X_train[cols], y_train, cv=rcv, scoring=SCORING, n_jobs=-1)
    rows.append({'feature set': name, 'AP': r['test_AP'].mean(), 'AP sd': r['test_AP'].std(), 'ROC-AUC': r['test_ROC_AUC'].mean()})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('feature set').round(3)

What I did.

  1. Five feature sets: all features; without Recency; without demographics (age, kids, teens, marital status, education); without both; without campaign history.
  2. For each: a fresh pipeline restricted to those columns, the same final settings (set_params(**one_se['params'])), scored with RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=3). Why repeated: 15 estimates per variant instead of 5, so small differences are less noisy.

Output (CV PR-AUC). All features 0.694; without Recency 0.621; without demographics 0.646; without both 0.578; without campaign history 0.547.

How to read the numbers – each value is the CV PR-AUC of the same model with fewer inputs (random = 0.147). The drop from 0.694 is the price of leaving that group out: campaign history −0.15 (the most valuable), Recency −0.07, demographics −0.05.

Decision: keep all features.

  • Highest accuracy, and every removal has a measurable cost.
  • Recency is only a risk if it was measured after the campaign – then customers who accepted would look "recent" because they accepted, which is leakage. That is a question for the data owner; the no-Recency model (0.62, still 4× random) is ready as a fallback.
  • Demographics: dropping them would not remove bias, because income and basket mix act as proxies for family status and age. So I keep them and audit the outcomes by group instead (next cell).

Risks before production (Q5d)¶

What I did – step by step

  1. cross_val_predict(final_model, X, y, cv=StratifiedKFold(5)) on all 1,975 labelled customers. Every customer gets a score from a model that didn't see them. Why: group-level rates need more customers than the 395 in the test set.
  2. Selected = score ≥ 0.26. For each group – age band, children, in a couple, education, income quartile – I compute:
    • the actual response rate;
    • the share selected for the offer;
    • the true positive rate – of the group's actual responders, how many the model selects;
    • the precision of the selection.

Output and what it means.

  • Selection rates: 34% of childless households vs 13% / 8% of families with 1 / 2+ children; 34% of the richest quarter vs 11–13% of everyone else; 26% of singles vs 13% of couples.
  • Among actual responders, it finds 79% of the childless ones but only 50% of those in families with 2+ children.

How to read the numbers

  • Selection rate – the share of a group that would receive the offer. Different selection rates are not unfair by themselves if the groups really respond differently – compare it with the group's actual response rate.
  • True positive rate – of the group's real responders, the share the model picks. This is the fairness number: equal TPRs mean that a customer who would accept has the same chance of being offered, whatever their group. 79% vs 50% means responsive large families are missed more often.
  • Precision – of the selected customers in a group, the share who accept; above 27.3% the selection pays for itself in that group.

Risks to flag before using this model to hand out discounts:

  • Fairness: discounts would flow to the richest, childless customers – who would probably buy anyway – and responsive families are missed more often. That is a reputational and regulatory risk.
  • Response is not incrementality: the model predicts who accepts, not who accepts because of the offer. That calls for a randomised holdout and an uplift model.
  • Feedback loop: keep 5–10% of contacts random, so the model keeps learning about everyone.
  • Economics: use margin, including the cost of the discount – not revenue.
  • Governance and data: GDPR rules on profiling, a possible Recency timing leak, data from 2012–14 and a small sample – so monitor calibration and retrain regularly.

Conclusions – Q5

  • A simple, explainable model wins. Logistic regression predicts who will accept the next campaign better than random forest and gradient boosting: ROC-AUC 0.91, PR-AUC 0.66 (vs 0.15 for random), and its top 10% respond 4.4× more than average.
  • Used with the break-even rule (contact only if the predicted chance is above 27%), it turns −1,385 into +484 per 1,000 customers, contacting only 18% of customers while still reaching 64% of responders.
  • The strongest signals: accepted an offer before, bought recently, buys by catalogue. Then tenure, and no teenagers at home.
  • Before using it to hand out discounts: it favours wealthy, childless customers; it predicts acceptance, not extra sales caused by the offer; and it needs monitoring and a check on Recency's timing.

In plain words for Marketing:

  • Stop mass campaigns.
  • Score every customer and contact only those the model rates above 27%.
  • Keep a small random control group to measure the true effect of each campaign.

Q6 — Customer segmentation¶

Task: cluster the customers, justify k, profile and name the segments, and propose an action for each.

In [54]:
# ═══ Q6 — Segmentation: scaling options ═══
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, AgglomerativeClustering
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score, calinski_harabasz_score, davies_bouldin_score, adjusted_rand_score
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

SEG_FEATURES = MNT_COLS + ['NumDealsPurchases', 'NumWebPurchases', 'NumCatalogPurchases', 'NumStorePurchases', 'NumWebVisitsMonth']
seg_raw = cust[SEG_FEATURES]

# Scaling options: (a) z-score on raw values, (b) log1p then z-score (chosen), (c) rank (quantile) then z-score
scalings = {
    'z-score (raw)': StandardScaler().fit_transform(seg_raw),
    'log1p + z-score': StandardScaler().fit_transform(np.log1p(seg_raw)),
    'rank + z-score': StandardScaler().fit_transform(seg_raw.rank(pct=True)),
}
rows = []
for name, Z in scalings.items():
    lbl = KMeans(4, n_init=20, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit_predict(Z)
    sizes = np.bincount(lbl)
    rows.append({'scaling': name, 'silhouette (k=4)': silhouette_score(Z, lbl), 'smallest cluster': sizes.min(),
                 'largest cluster': sizes.max()})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('scaling').round(3))
Z = scalings['log1p + z-score']

What I did – step by step

  1. SEG_FEATURES – the 11 behaviour columns: 6 spend categories, deal / web / catalogue / store purchases, and web visits.
    • Demographics left out on purpose, so I can use them afterwards to validate the segments.
    • Recency left out because it is flat and changes every day, while a persona should be stable.
  2. Three scalings, all with StandardScaler() (mean 0, SD 1): on raw values, on np.log1p values, and on ranks (rank(pct=True)). Why scale at all: k-means uses distances, so without scaling the column with the biggest numbers (wine spend) would dominate.
  3. KMeans(4, n_init=20, random_state=42) on each version. Why n_init=20: k-means depends on its random starting points, so it runs 20 times and keeps the best solution.
  4. Compared the silhouette_score and the cluster sizes.

Why k-means – and why I could use it here

  • k-means groups customers so that each one is as close as possible to its cluster's average profile – which directly gives "personas" with a readable average profile.
  • What it needs, and how this data meets it:
    • numeric features ✓ (spend amounts and purchase counts);
    • features on comparable scales – ensured by the standardisation ✓;
    • distances that make sense – after log1p a step from 10 to 100 counts like a step from 100 to 1,000, so a few heavy spenders don't dominate ✓;
    • roughly round clusters of similar spread – this can't be guaranteed in advance, so I cross-check with a Gaussian mixture (any elliptical shape) and Ward clustering in the next cell and in the Appendix.

Output and what it means. Silhouette 0.31 (raw), 0.25 (log), 0.25 (rank). Smallest cluster: 260 customers on raw values vs 407 with logs.

How to read the numbers

  • Silhouette – for each customer: (distance to the nearest other cluster − distance to its own cluster) ÷ the larger of the two, averaged over everyone. From −1 to 1: near 1 = clearly in the right cluster, 0 = on the border, negative = probably in the wrong one. Kaufman & Rousseeuw's rule of thumb: above 0.7 strong, 0.5–0.7 reasonable, 0.25–0.5 weak structure, below 0.25 no substantial structure.
  • Important: the three silhouettes are measured in three different spaces (raw, log, rank), so they can't be compared with each other – a higher raw silhouette doesn't mean a better segmentation.

Decision: log + standardisation.

  • With logs, going from 10 to 100 counts as much as going from 100 to 1,000 – how a marketer thinks about spend – and a few heavy spenders don't dominate the distances.
  • Because the silhouettes can't be compared across spaces, the choice rests on that logic, and log scaling also gives the more balanced clusters (smallest 407 vs 260 customers).

# Choosing k: four internal criteria + stability + two alternative algorithms
ks = range(2, 11)
rows = []
rng = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE)
for k in ks:
    km = KMeans(k, n_init=20, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(Z)
    gmm = GaussianMixture(k, covariance_type='full', n_init=3, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(Z)
    ward = AgglomerativeClustering(k, linkage='ward').fit_predict(Z)
    aris = []
    for b in range(20):     # stability: refit on bootstrap samples, compare labels on the full data
        idx = rng.integers(0, len(Z), len(Z))
        km_b = KMeans(k, n_init=5, random_state=b).fit(Z[idx])
        aris.append(adjusted_rand_score(km.labels_, km_b.predict(Z)))
    rows.append({'k': k, 'inertia': km.inertia_, 'silhouette': silhouette_score(Z, km.labels_),

What I did – step by step. For every k from 2 to 10:

  1. KMeans(k, n_init=20).fit(Z), recording:
    • inertia_ – the within-cluster sum of squares, for the elbow chart;
    • silhouette_score;
    • calinski_harabasz_score;
    • davies_bouldin_score.
  2. Stability: 20 times, refit k-means on a bootstrap sample (rng.integers row indices) and compare its labels on the full data with the original solution using adjusted_rand_score (ARI).
  3. Two other algorithms as cross-checks:
    • GaussianMixture(k, covariance_type='full') with BIC – allows elliptical clusters of different sizes;
    • AgglomerativeClustering(k, linkage='ward') – hierarchical clustering, with its agreement with k-means measured by ARI.
  4. The smallest cluster's share of customers – a segment that is too small isn't worth a separate campaign.

Why several criteria – and why I could use them here

  • There is no single "correct" number of clusters; each criterion measures something different, so I look for agreement and business usefulness.
  • Silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Davies-Bouldin need a meaningful distance – Euclidean distance on log-transformed, standardised features ✓.
  • Bootstrap ARI resamples customers – needs independent customers ✓.
  • Gaussian-mixture BIC assumes the data is a blend of bell-shaped clouds. That is only partly true here: many customers have exactly zero in some columns (26% never buy by catalogue; 17–19% buy no fruit, fish or sweets), and such spikes break the bell shape. So I read the BIC with care (see below).
  • Ward builds clusters bottom-up with a different algorithm – an independent check that the structure isn't an artefact of k-means.

How to read this chart (the orange vertical line marks the chosen k = 4)

  1. Elbow: X = number of clusters k; Y = within-cluster sum of squares (how far customers are from their own cluster's centre, in total). It always falls as k grows; look for the bend where adding a cluster stops helping much.
  2. Silhouette: higher = better-separated clusters.
  3. Stability (bootstrap ARI): 1 = the same clusters every time the data is resampled; lower = the clusters change with the sample.
  4. GMM BIC: lower = the Gaussian mixture describes the data better.

What I read from it

  1. Elbow: the biggest drop is 2 → 3 (12,033 → 9,415), then 8,587 at k = 4 and 7,878 at k = 5; after that the curve is smooth. The bend is around k = 3–4, with no sharp elbow.
  2. Silhouette: falls steadily – 0.38 (k = 2) → 0.31 → 0.25 (k = 4) → 0.19 → 0.14 (k = 10) – with no peak above k = 2. The customer base is a continuum, not separate islands.
  3. Stability: 0.97–0.98 for k = 2–3, 0.87 at k = 4, 0.91 at k = 5, then it drops to 0.67–0.77 for k ≥ 6 → more than 5 clusters is unstable.
  4. GMM BIC: nearly flat for k = 2–4 (41.4k → 39.5k), a big drop at k = 5–6 (29.7k, 25.0k), then flat. The mixture "prefers" 6+ components. I checked what the extra components are: they mainly separate customers with exactly zero in a column – e.g. at k = 6 one component is 508 light buyers who all have zero catalogue purchases, next to 426 light buyers who all have at least one. Fitting those spikes improves the density fit, but it isn't a different behaviour to act on – and at k = 6 stability falls to 0.77.

Output and what it means.

  • The silhouette is highest at k = 2 (0.38) and falls steadily – there is no sharp "natural" number of clusters.
  • Stability is 0.97–0.98 for k = 2–3, 0.87 at k = 4 and 0.91 at k = 5.
  • The smallest segment is 47% / 29% / 20% / 18% of customers for k = 2 / 3 / 4 / 5.

How to read the numbers

  • Silhouette (−1 to 1) – Kaufman & Rousseeuw's scale: above 0.7 strong, 0.5–0.7 reasonable, 0.25–0.5 weak, below 0.25 no substantial structure. 0.25 at k = 4 is at that border – honest reading: the segments are a useful way to cut a continuum into actionable groups, not naturally separated groups.
  • Calinski-Harabasz – spread between clusters ÷ spread within them; higher = better (1,031 at k = 4).
  • Davies-Bouldin – how similar each cluster is to its most similar neighbour; lower = better, 0 = perfectly separated (1.59 at k = 4).
  • ARI (adjusted Rand index) – agreement between two clusterings: 1 = identical, 0 = no better than chance. Steinley's scale: ≥ 0.90 excellent, 0.80–0.90 good, 0.65–0.80 moderate, below 0.65 poor. Stability 0.87 at k = 4 = good; agreement with Ward 0.71 = moderate.
  • Note: silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz and Davies-Bouldin all favour k = 2 – but k = 2 only splits light from heavy buyers, which we already knew from Q3a.

Decision: 4 segments.

  • k = 2 only splits light buyers from heavy buyers.
  • k = 3 merges the deal-seeking teen parents with the affluent families.
  • k = 5 only splits the low spenders into 41 vs 105 with an identical profile – no new action.
  • k = 4 is stable (0.87), every segment holds at least 20% of customers, it agrees with Ward (ARI 0.71), and each segment needs a different action.

# ═══ Q6 — Final k-means (k = 4) and segment profiles ═══
K = 4
SEG_NAMES = {0: 'Budget Young Families', 1: 'Deal-Seeking Teen Parents', 2: 'Established Family Foodies',
             3: 'Affluent Childless Connoisseurs'}   # named AFTER reading the profile below
km = KMeans(K, n_init=50, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(Z)
# order clusters by average spend so the labels are stable and readable (0 = lowest spend)
order = pd.Series(cust['MntTotal'].to_numpy()).groupby(km.labels_).mean().sort_values().index
relabel = {old: new for new, old in enumerate(order)}
cust['Segment'] = pd.Series(km.labels_, index=cust.index).map(relabel)

}).T.astype(float).round(2)
channel_mix = g[CHANNEL_COLS].sum().div(g['ChannelPurchases'].sum(), axis=0)

for c in CHANNEL_COLS:

over_index = (channel_mix / base_mix).idxmax(axis=1).str.replace('Num', '').str.replace('Purchases', '')
profile = profile.astype(object)
profile.loc['most over-indexed channel'] = over_index.values
profile.loc['expected profit per contact (MU)'] = [round(REVENUE_PER_RESPONSE * r - COST_PER_CONTACT, 2) for r in g['Response'].mean()]
profile.loc['response vs break-even'] = [f'{r:.0%} vs {BREAK_EVEN_RATE:.0%}' for r in g['Response'].mean()]

What I did – step by step

  1. KMeans(4, n_init=50) – more restarts for the final solution.
  2. Relabelled the clusters 0–3 by average spend. k-means numbers clusters arbitrarily, so this keeps the labels readable and stable.
  3. The profile: groupby('Segment') for size, share of revenue, income, age, share with young kids and with teenagers, spend per category, average order value, purchases per channel, deal share, web visits, earlier acceptances, response rate, and expected profit per contact = 11 × response rate − 3.
  4. Channel mix: each channel's share of the segment's purchases, plus the channel most over-represented compared with the whole base.
  5. Named the segments only after reading the profile.

Output – four personas:

Segment Customers / revenue Profile Action
Budget Young Families 36% / 4% income ~32k, 77% have young kids, ~12 per order, 34% of purchases on deal, browse the web a lot but buy in store; response 7% no paid outreach – owned channels, family bundles
Deal-Seeking Teen Parents 21% / 16% income ~49k, 75% have teenagers, wine ~70% of the basket, most deal purchases, web deal-led wine offers online, only to model-selected customers
Established Family Foodies 20% / 34% income ~63k, ~1,000 spend across all categories, omnichannel, few deals cross-sell fresh and premium food; loyalty points rather than discounts
Affluent Childless Connoisseurs 22% / 47% income ~76k, 84% without children, highest spend (1,300) and order value (~71), catalogue, almost no deals; response 25% VIP and retention programme, no discounts

How to read the numbers

  • Customers / revenue – the segment's share of the customer base vs its share of revenue. Revenue share far above customer share = a high-value segment (Connoisseurs 22% → 47%); far below = low value (Young Families 36% → 4%).
  • Expected profit per contact = 11 × response rate − 3 – what one contact earns on average. Positive only if the response rate is above 27.3%.
  • Demographics in the profile (income, kids, age) were not used to build the clusters – so if the segments differ clearly on them, that is independent evidence that the segments are real.

Key insight. Even the best segment responds at 25% – below the 27% break-even – so the expected profit per contact is negative for every segment (−2.2 to −0.25).

What I did. PCA(2) projects the 11 dimensions onto the 2 directions with the most variation, only to draw the segments – the clustering itself used all 11 features. Each panel highlights one segment over the others in grey. The loadings table shows what each axis means.

Why PCA – and why I could use it here. It is the standard way to draw many dimensions on a flat chart. It needs numeric features on comparable scales – the same log + standardised features as the clustering ✓ (without scaling, wine spend alone would define the first axis). It is used for display only – no test and no conclusion rests on it.

How to read this chart

  • Each dot is one customer, placed by its two PCA scores; the positions are identical in all four panels. In each panel one segment is blue and everyone else is grey.
  • X axis – PC1 (57% of the variation) = "how much the customer buys": all spend columns and web / catalogue / store purchases load positively on it (0.29–0.37), deal purchases not at all (0.00) and web visits negatively (−0.23). Left = buys little, right = buys a lot.
  • Y axis – PC2 (15%) = "deal-hunting and browsing": it loads on deal purchases (0.68), web visits (0.49) and web purchases (0.39). Up = many deals and visits, down = few.
  • Where a blue cloud sits describes the segment; a little overlap at the edges is normal, because the clustering used all 11 dimensions and the chart shows only 2.

What I read from it

  • 0 – Budget Young Families: far left (low buying), middle height → small baskets, average deal use (1.7 deal purchases).
  • 1 – Deal-Seeking Teen Parents: centre-left and the highest on PC2 → moderate buying with the most deals (3.9) and web visits (6.6 a month).
  • 2 – Established Family Foodies: right of centre, slightly above zero → high buying with some deals (3.1).
  • 3 – Affluent Childless Connoisseurs: far right and the lowest on PC2 → the highest buying with the fewest deals (1.0) and web visits (2.1).
  • The four clouds occupy different regions with only thin overlap at their borders.

Output and what it means.

  • The 2 components show 72% of the variation (57% + 15%), so the picture is a fair summary of the 11 dimensions.
  • The segments differ along two business dimensions – volume and deal orientation – which is exactly what their names and actions are built on.

How to read the numbers

  • Explained variance 57% / 15% – how much of the differences between customers each axis captures; together 72%, so 28% is not visible in the picture.
  • Loadings (−1 to 1) – how strongly each original column contributes to an axis and in which direction; a large absolute value = that column defines the axis.

Conclusions – Q6

  • Four stable segments (bootstrap ARI 0.87), based purely on buying behaviour and validated by demographics: Budget Young Families, Deal-Seeking Teen Parents, Established Family Foodies, Affluent Childless Connoisseurs.
  • Value is extremely uneven: 22% of customers bring in 47% of revenue, while the largest segment (36%) brings in only 4%.
  • Honest caveat: customers form a continuum (silhouette 0.25), so the four segments are a practical, reproducible cut for planning campaigns – customers near a border may resemble the neighbouring segment.
  • No segment responds above the 27% break-even on average. Segments decide the message and the channel; the Q5 model decides who within each segment is contacted.

In plain words for Marketing:

  • Connoisseurs: a VIP / retention programme with premium selections, no discounts.
  • Young families: value bundles through free channels (website and app), no paid campaigns.
  • Teen parents: deal-led wine offers online.
  • Family foodies: premium cross-sell and loyalty points.

Q7 — SQL & turning this into a recurring report¶

Task: SQL for average spend and response rate by education; how to make this a weekly report.

In [58]:
# ═══ Q7a — SQL: textbook vs production query, validated against pandas ═══
# Run both queries against an in-memory SQLite copy of the RAW file, and check them against pandas.
con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
df.to_sql('customer_marketing', con, index=False)

literal_sql = """
SELECT Education,
       AVG(MntTotal)                AS avg_mnt_total,
       AVG(CAST(Response AS REAL))  AS response_rate
FROM customer_marketing_with_education
GROUP BY Education
ORDER BY avg_mnt_total DESC;
"""
production_sql = """
WITH deduplicated AS (                        -- 184 exact copies in the source
    SELECT DISTINCT * FROM customer_marketing
),
base AS (
    SELECT
        CASE
            WHEN education_Basic        = 1 THEN 'Basic'
            WHEN "education_2n Cycle"   = 1 THEN '2n Cycle'
            WHEN education_Graduation   = 1 THEN 'Graduation'
            WHEN education_Master       = 1 THEN 'Master'
            WHEN education_PhD          = 1 THEN 'PhD'
        END AS education,
        -- recompute: the delivered MntTotal silently excludes gold
        MntWines + MntFruits + MntMeatProducts + MntFishProducts + MntSweetProducts + MntGoldProds AS mnt_total,
        Response
    FROM deduplicated
)
SELECT
    education,
    COUNT(*)                                        AS customers,
    ROUND(AVG(mnt_total), 1)                        AS avg_mnt_total,
    ROUND(100.0 * AVG(CAST(Response AS REAL)), 1)   AS response_rate_pct
FROM base
GROUP BY education
ORDER BY avg_mnt_total DESC;
"""
# The literal query needs an Education column -> expose it through a view built from the flags
con.execute("""CREATE VIEW customer_marketing_with_education AS
               SELECT *, CASE WHEN education_Basic = 1 THEN 'Basic' WHEN "education_2n Cycle" = 1 THEN '2n Cycle'
                              WHEN education_Graduation = 1 THEN 'Graduation' WHEN education_Master = 1 THEN 'Master'
                              ELSE 'PhD' END AS Education
               FROM customer_marketing""")
literal = pd.read_sql(literal_sql, con)
production = pd.read_sql(production_sql, con)

# Cross-check the production query against pandas on the de-duplicated raw file
chk = df.drop_duplicates().assign(education=lambda d: d[EDU_COLS].idxmax(axis=1).str.replace('education_', ''),
                                  mnt_total=lambda d: d[MNT_COLS].sum(axis=1))
chk = chk.groupby('education').agg(customers=('Response', 'size'), avg_mnt_total=('mnt_total', 'mean'),
                                   response_rate_pct=('Response', 'mean'))
chk['response_rate_pct'] *= 100
merged = production.set_index('education').join(chk, rsuffix='_pandas')
assert np.allclose(merged['avg_mnt_total'], merged['avg_mnt_total_pandas'].round(1))
assert np.allclose(merged['response_rate_pct'], merged['response_rate_pct_pandas'].round(1))
assert (merged['customers'] == merged['customers_pandas']).all()
print('Production query matches pandas exactly.\n\nLiteral query on the raw table (duplicates + MntTotal without gold):')
display(literal.round(3))
print('Production query (de-duplicated, corrected MntTotal):')
display(production)
print('Same metric on the fully cleaned table from Q1 (pandas):')
cust.groupby('Education', observed=True).agg(customers=('MntTotal', 'size'), avg_mnt_total=('MntTotal', 'mean'),
                                             response_rate_pct=('Response', 'mean')).assign(
    response_rate_pct=lambda t: 100 * t['response_rate_pct']).sort_values('avg_mnt_total', ascending=False).round(1)

What I did – step by step

  1. sqlite3.connect(':memory:') + df.to_sql('customer_marketing', con) – an in-memory database holding the raw table. Why: the SQL is actually executed and checked, not just written.
  2. The textbook query – AVG(MntTotal) and AVG(CAST(Response AS REAL)) grouped by Education. It runs against a view I created (CREATE VIEW ... CASE WHEN ...), because the raw table has no Education column, only one-hot flags.
  3. The production query, built from two CTEs (WITH ... AS):
    • SELECT DISTINCT * removes the 184 exact duplicates;
    • CASE WHEN education_Basic = 1 THEN 'Basic' ... turns the flags into one education column. "education_2n Cycle" is in double quotes because the column name contains a space;
    • the total is recomputed as the sum of all 6 categories, because the delivered MntTotal excludes gold;
    • AVG(CAST(Response AS REAL)) – some databases (e.g. SQL Server) average integers as integers and would return 0;
    • GROUP BY education ORDER BY avg_mnt_total DESC.
  4. pd.read_sql() fetches the results, and assert np.allclose(...) checks them against the same numbers computed in pandas – proof that the query is correct.
  5. For comparison, the same metric on the fully cleaned table from Q1.

Output and what it means.

  • The production query matches pandas exactly.
  • Fixing the data changes the ranking: on the raw table Master (571.0) edges out Graduation (570.9), but after the fixes Graduation (624.0) is ahead of Master (619.9). A report on the raw table would have shown the wrong order.
  • PhD has the highest spend and response rate on every version.

Weekly report – end to end (Q7b):

  1. Ingestion into a warehouse, with campaign contacts and responses stored as time-stamped events.
  2. Transformation in dbt: totals always computed from their components, ages and tenure relative to the snapshot date, and metric definitions stored in one place.
  3. Weekly orchestration with Airflow, Dagster or dbt Cloud.
  4. A dashboard showing the response rate against the 27% break-even, campaign profit and the segments.

Every Q1 issue becomes an automated test that stops the run before bad data reaches the dashboard:

  • unique customer IDs;
  • totals equal to the sum of their parts;
  • no negative spend;
  • exactly one education flag per customer;
  • valid age and income ranges;
  • data-freshness and drift alerts.

Conclusions – Q7

  • The SQL runs on the raw table and matches pandas exactly. Cleaning changes the ranking of education groups, so a report on uncleaned data would mislead.
  • A weekly report must rebuild every metric from the raw data and stop automatically when a data-quality check fails.

In plain words for Marketing: a dashboard is only as good as its data checks. Ask for the "data as of" date and the data-quality status on every report, and track campaign profit against the 27% break-even – not just the response rate.

Q8 — Executive summary for the CMO¶

To: CMO Re: What our customer data says about campaigns

Our last campaign went to everyone and lost money. Each contact costs 3 and each acceptance brings in 11, so a campaign must convince 27% of the people it reaches just to break even. We convinced 15%, losing almost half of what we spent.

Three findings explain why and what to do:

  • Value is concentrated. The top 20% of customers generate 52% of our revenue; the bottom half generates only 9%.
  • Past behaviour predicts response. Customers who accepted an earlier offer accept again 30–82% of the time; the 79% who never did accept only 8% of the time.
  • Family type matters. Households with teenagers respond far less, even at the same income.

Recommendations:

  1. Stop mass campaigns. Contact only customers our model rates above the 27% break-even. In testing, this turned a loss of 1,385 into a profit of about 480 per 1,000 customers.
  2. Launch a VIP programme for affluent customers without children: 22% of customers, 47% of revenue. Offer premium selections, not discounts.
  3. Fix the data. One record in ten is a duplicate, which distorts every dashboard.

from sklearn.preprocessing import SplineTransformer
checks = []

# 1. Independence of observations (every test, bootstrap and CV split assumes one row per customer)
id_cols = [c for c in FEATURES_NO_TARGET if c in cust.columns and c not in MARITAL_COLS]
checks.append(('Independence', 'duplicate customers left in the analytical table', int(cust.duplicated(subset=id_cols).sum()), '= 0'))

# 2. Chi-square validity: expected count in every cell >= 5
checks.append(('Chi-square (children x response)', 'smallest expected cell count',
               round(resp_tests.loc['min_expected_count'].min(), 1), '>= 5'))
checks.append(('Chi-square (complaint x response)', 'smallest expected cell count',
               round(complain['min_expected_count'], 1), '>= 5 (else use Fisher exact)'))
checks.append(('Chi-square goodness of fit (Recency)', 'smallest expected count per 10-day bin', round(len(cust) / 10, 1), '>= 5'))

# 3. CMH common odds ratio assumes a similar odds ratio in every income quartile -> likelihood-ratio test of the interaction
def logit_loglik(Xd, yv):
    res = logit_inference(Xd, yv)
    Xc = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Xd)), np.asarray(Xd, float)])
    pr = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-Xc @ res['coef'].to_numpy()))
    yv = np.asarray(yv, float)
    return np.sum(yv * np.log(pr) + (1 - yv) * np.log(1 - pr))

qd = pd.get_dummies(lab['IncomeQuartile'], prefix='q', drop_first=True).astype(float)
base_X = pd.concat([lab[['HasChildren']].astype(float), qd], axis=1)
inter_X = pd.concat([base_X, qd.mul(lab['HasChildren'], axis=0).add_prefix('kids_x_')], axis=1)
lr_stat = 2 * (logit_loglik(inter_X, lab['Response']) - logit_loglik(base_X, lab['Response']))
p_homog = stats.chi2.sf(lr_stat, qd.shape[1])
or_by_q = {str(q): float(round((t[0, 0] * t[1, 1]) / (t[0, 1] * t[1, 0]), 2)) for q, t in zip(lab['IncomeQuartile'].cat.categories, tables)}
checks.append(('CMH homogeneity of odds ratios', f'odds ratio (kids vs none) per income quartile {or_by_q}; LR test of interaction',
               f'p = {p_homog:.3f}', 'p > 0.05 = homogeneous'))

# 4. Events per variable for the logistic regressions (rule of thumb: >= 10 for an UNpenalised model)
n_par_q5 = len(lr_1se.named_steps['prep'].get_feature_names_out())
checks.append(('EPV, Q4 logistic models', 'responders / parameters (3 to 11 parameters)',
               f'{lab["Response"].sum() / 11:.0f} to {lab["Response"].sum() / 3:.0f}', '>= 10'))

               round(y_train.sum() / n_par_q5, 1), '>= 10, otherwise regularise'))

# 5. Multicollinearity (variance inflation factors)
design = make_preprocessor().fit(X_train)
M = design.transform(X_train)

def vif_values(Mx, names):
    out = []
    for j in range(Mx.shape[1]):
        A = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Mx)), np.delete(Mx, j, axis=1)])
        beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, Mx[:, j], rcond=None)
        r2 = 1 - ((Mx[:, j] - A @ beta) ** 2).sum() / ((Mx[:, j] - Mx[:, j].mean()) ** 2).sum()
        out.append(1 / (1 - r2))
    return pd.Series(out, index=names)

vif = vif_values(M, design.get_feature_names_out()).sort_values(ascending=False)
checks.append(('Multicollinearity (Q5 inputs)', f'largest VIFs: { {k: float(v) for k, v in vif.head(3).round(1).items()} }', round(vif.max(), 1),
               '< 10 ideal; higher -> regularise'))
vif_q4 = vif_values(np.column_stack([lab['HasChildren'], lab['Income'] / 1e4, lab['Age'] / 10]), ['HasChildren', 'Income', 'Age'])
checks.append(('Multicollinearity (Q4 controls)', 'largest VIF of HasChildren / Income / Age', round(vif_q4.max(), 2), '< 5'))

What I did – step by step (each check tests one assumption of a method used above)

  1. Independence – every test, bootstrap and CV split assumes one row per customer: cust.duplicated(subset=...) on the cleaned table.
  2. Chi-square validity – at least 5 expected per cell: the smallest expected count from chi2_contingency.
  3. The same effect in every income band – needed for one pooled odds ratio. A likelihood-ratio test: logit_loglik() gives the log-likelihood of a logistic model with and without "children × income quartile" interaction terms, and stats.chi2.sf(2 × difference, 3) gives the p-value.
  4. Events per parameter – the rule of thumb is ≥ 10 for an unpenalised logistic regression: responders / number of coefficients.
  5. Multicollinearity (VIF): each feature regressed on all the others with np.linalg.lstsq; VIF = 1 / (1 − R²).
  6. Linearity of the log-odds: the same logistic regression with SplineTransformer(n_knots=4, degree=3), which lets every numeric feature bend freely, tuned with GridSearchCV on the same folds, compared with the linear version.
  7. k-means assumptions (compact, round clusters): agreement (ARI) with a GaussianMixture(covariance_type='full'), which allows any elliptical shape, and with Ward.
  8. Calibration: the Brier score vs a naive guess.

Why the likelihood-ratio test for check 3 – and why I could use it. It compares two nested logistic models (with and without the 3 interaction terms) fitted by maximum likelihood on the same customers ✓. Twice the difference in log-likelihood then follows a χ² distribution with 3 degrees of freedom (one per extra term) – valid with large samples and enough events ✓ (291 responders). It is the standard test of "does the effect differ between groups?"

Output and what it means.

  • Independence: 0 duplicates ✓.
  • Chi-square: 82 expected for children ✓, but only 2.8 for complaints ✗ – which is why Fisher's exact test was used there.
  • Same effect across income bands: p = 0.007 ✗ – odds ratio 1.08 in the lowest quartile vs 0.22–0.38 in the others, which is why the effect is reported per band.
  • Events per parameter: 26–97 for the Q4 models ✓, but only 7.3 for the Q5 model ✗ – which is why it is regularised.
  • VIF: up to 24 for the Q5 inputs (order value 24.2, wine 17.9, meat 11.8) – handled by the elastic net, which zeroed order value. For the Q4 controls, VIF ≤ 1.3 ✓.
  • Linearity: spline 0.698 vs 0.702 linear – curves add nothing ✓.
  • k-means: ARI 0.71 with Ward (moderate agreement) and 0.59 with the Gaussian mixture (below "moderate") – the main split by volume and deal orientation is shared, but the exact borders depend on the algorithm. Together with the silhouette of 0.25 this says: a stable, useful partition of a continuum, not naturally separated groups (stability 0.87).
  • PCA: 72% of the variation in 2 components – used only for drawing.
  • Calibration: Brier 0.080 vs 0.125 ✓.

How to read the numbers

  • p = 0.007 (homogeneity) – here a small p is bad news for the assumption: it means the odds ratios really differ between income bands (p > 0.05 would mean "consistent with one common effect").
  • Events per parameter (EPV) – responders ÷ estimated coefficients. Below ~10 an unpenalised logistic regression gives unstable, exaggerated coefficients; regularisation fixes this.
  • VIF (variance inflation factor) – how much a coefficient's uncertainty is inflated because that input can be predicted from the others. 1 = not at all; above 5 = worrying; above 10 = serious. 24 = order value is almost a combination of the spend columns.
  • ARI – 1 = identical clusterings, 0 = chance agreement; ≥ 0.90 excellent, 0.80–0.90 good, 0.65–0.80 moderate, below 0.65 poor (Steinley).
  • Brier score – 0 = perfect; 0.125 = always predicting the 14.7% average; 0.080 = 36% better.

Conclusions – method checks

  • Every method used is valid on this data, or was adapted where an assumption failed:
    • Fisher instead of chi-square for complaints;
    • per-band reporting instead of one pooled odds ratio;
    • regularisation for the few events per parameter and the correlated spend features.
  • The model's linear form was cross-checked against a flexible spline model and holds up. The k-means segments are stable (bootstrap ARI 0.87) and partly reproduced by other algorithms (Ward 0.71, Gaussian mixture 0.59): a useful, reproducible way to cut a continuum of customers into actionable groups, not naturally separated groups.
